title: Toward adaptive cyborg tissues.
authors: Qiang Li; Jeantine Lunshof; Jia Liu
abstract: ['Organoids and engineered tissues have emerged as powerful models of human biology, yet their development and function are often characterized through endpoint measurements that provide only static snapshots of dynamic biological processes. Recent advances in stretchable mesh electronics, developmental biointegration, and organoid engineering have enabled the creation of cyborg tissues with embedded sensing, stimulation, and computational capabilities. This review highlights recent progress in developmental bioelectronic integration, multifunctional tissue mapping, biological state reconstruction, and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled cyborg systems. We discuss how embedded bioelectronics can be combined with molecular and spatial profiling technologies to characterize tissue function, developmental trajectories, and biological states. These advances establish cyborg tissues as biologically integrated platforms for regenerative medicine, disease modeling, drug discovery, and adaptive biotechnology.']

title: Engineering human multi-organ tissue chip niches for drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity prediction.
authors: Jiawei Li; Sofia Madrigal Gamboa; Jade T Chao; Sarah C Heilshorn; Joseph C Wu
abstract: ['Predicting human drug responses in vitro remains a central challenge in drug development. Animal models have shown limited accuracy in recapitulating human drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity, which arise from coordinated activities across multiple organs. Multi-organ-on-a-chip systems (mOoCs) are a class of promising new approach methodologies that can reconstruct these inter-organ processes. Existing mOoCs have demonstrated proof of concept for inter-organ coupling but translation-ready systems remain out of reach. Two key challenges persist: how to preserve the distinct biochemical and biomechanical niches of each organ while enabling controlled exchange between them, and how to develop mOoCs into robust translation-ready systems. In this Review, we first summarize progress in niche-preserving engineering strategies developed within single-organ systems and outline how these components are integrated to reconstruct multi-organ niches. We then highlight scalable manufacturing and multimodal readouts as the basis for making mOoCs into robust, reproducible and data-rich technologies for drug response evaluation. In the future, the resulting human-relevant datasets are expected to interface with artificial intelligence workflows to accelerate next-generation drug discovery.']

title: Invisible Infrastructure at Risk: Funding Crises Threaten Global Bioscience Research.
authors: Valerie Wood; Elspeth A Bruford; Steven J Marygold; Valerie B O'Donnell; Katja Röper; Jamie A Davies; Christine Orengo; Paul Nurse; Neil Hall
abstract: ['Modern biology depends on invisible infrastructure that is essential yet precariously funded. Millions of biological observations are interpreted through resources that sit beneath routine scientific practice, largely unseen in everyday research. Every experiment, genome analysis, AI model, and clinical interpretation relies on these biological knowledgebases, which most researchers rarely notice until they disappear. That infrastructure is now under threat. Across the world, the biological databases that underpin modern research, built over decades of public and charitable investment, face severe and increasing financial instability. This crisis arrives at a particularly damaging moment: many governments have identified life sciences as a strategic growth sector and are investing heavily in genomics, AI-enabled drug discovery, and precision medicine. Yet every one of these ambitions ultimately depends on curated biological data resources reliant on emergency bridge grants, donations, staff secondments, and ad hoc rescue efforts.']

title: Development of proteome-derived cyclic peptide libraries via ortho-phthalaldehyde-assisted cyclization.
authors: Ying Wei; Kangze Feng; Wenxuan Hou; Xiaolin Tian; Yuanyuan Xue; Wenhao Zhang; Haiteng Deng
abstract: ['Cyclic peptides possess unique structural features and binding capabilities that make them attractive scaffolds for molecular recognition. title: Beyond Antibodies: Glypican-3-Targeting Peptides for Precision Hepatocellular Carcinoma Theranostics.
authors: Narendra Raju Nagpure; Nitesh Mani Tripathi; Neelam Verma; Anupam Bandyopadhyay
journal: Journal of peptide science : an official publication of the European Peptide Society
abstract: ['Glypican-3 (GPC-3) is a cell-surface glycoprotein, highly expressed in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) but largely absent in normal adult liver tissues, making it a clinically compelling biomarker and therapeutic target. Although monoclonal antibodies and antibody-drug conjugates have proven to be GPC-3-targeted therapies, their large molecular size, slow pharmacokinetics, and potential immunogenicity limit their diagnostic applications. Peptide ligands offer an attractive alternative owing to their low molecular weight, rapid tumor penetration, favorable clearance profiles, synthetic accessibility, and ease of chemical modification. This topical review highlights the development of linear and cyclic GPC-3-binding peptides over the past two decades, developed primarily via phage display, rational optimization, and structure-guided approaches, enabling PET, SPECT, and fluorescence imaging of HCC in preclinical models. Recent refinements, including albumin-binding modifications and cyclization strategies, have improved tumor-to-liver contrast and in\xa0vivo stability. This review summarizes the biological significance of GPC-3, compares peptides and peptide probes as targeting modalities, and critically analyzes recent advances in linear and cyclic peptide-based GPC-3 imaging probes. We also emphasized the importance, current challenges, and future opportunities in AI/ML-based design of peptide ligands for HCC theranostics.']

title: Engineering human multi-organ tissue chip niches for drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity prediction.
authors: Jiawei Li; Sofia Madrigal Gamboa; Jade T Chao; Sarah C Heilshorn; Joseph C Wu
abstract: ['Predicting human drug responses in vitro remains a central challenge in drug development. Animal models have shown limited accuracy in recapitulating human drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity, which arise from coordinated activities across multiple organs. Multi-organ-on-a-chip systems (mOoCs) are a class of promising new approach methodologies that can reconstruct these inter-organ processes. Existing mOoCs have demonstrated proof of concept for inter-organ coupling but translation-ready systems remain out of reach. Two key challenges persist: how to preserve the distinct biochemical and biomechanical niches of each organ while enabling controlled exchange between them, and how to develop mOoCs into robust translation-ready systems. In this Review, we first summarize progress in niche-preserving engineering strategies developed within single-organ systems and outline how these components are integrated to reconstruct multi-organ niches. We then highlight scalable manufacturing and multimodal readouts as the basis for making mOoCs into robust, reproducible and data-rich technologies for drug response evaluation. In the future, the resulting human-relevant datasets are expected to interface with artificial intelligence workflows to accelerate next-generation drug discovery.']

title: Invisible Infrastructure at Risk: Funding Crises Threaten Global Bioscience Research.
authors: Valerie Wood; Elspeth A Bruford; Steven J Marygold; Valerie B O'Donnell; Katja Röper; Jamie A Davies; Christine Orengo; Paul Nurse; Neil Hall
abstract: ['Modern biology depends on invisible infrastructure that is essential yet precariously funded. Millions of biological observations are interpreted through resources that sit beneath routine scientific practice, largely unseen in everyday research. Every experiment, genome analysis, AI model, and clinical interpretation relies on these biological knowledgebases, which most researchers rarely notice until they disappear. That infrastructure is now under threat. Across the world, the biological databases that underpin modern research, built over decades of public and charitable investment, face severe and increasing financial instability. This crisis arrives at a particularly damaging moment: many governments have identified life sciences as a strategic growth sector and are investing heavily in genomics, AI-enabled drug discovery, and precision medicine. Yet every one of these ambitions ultimately depends on curated biological data resources reliant on emergency bridge grants, donations, staff secondments, and ad hoc rescue efforts.']

title: Deep generative models in biological sequence and structure analysis and design.
authors: Fahimeh Palizban; Mohammadmahdi Sarbishegi; Huiqi Qu; Amir Hossein Saeidian; Mahya Mehrmohamadi; Joseph Glessner; Hakon Hakonarson
abstract: ['Deep generative models have transformed biological sequence modeling from predictive analysis toward increasingly controllable design. Early biological applications of Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) established latent representation learning and sequence synthesis, while recent advances in transformer-based language models, discrete diffusion, flow-matching, and multimodal generative frameworks have substantially expanded the scope of biological design. This review examines generative models for DNA, RNA, and protein sequence design, emphasizing how different model classes represent biological constraints, operate over discrete and continuous spaces, and integrate sequence, structure, and function. We compare VAEs, GANs, autoregressive and masked language models, diffusion models, and flow-based approaches across genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics, with particular attention to controllability, long-range dependency modeling, structural grounding, generalization, and experimental utility. We further examine evaluation strategies, out-of-distribution generalization, and closed-loop design-build-test-learn workflows that connect in silico generation with empirical validation. We distinguish fundamental modality-dependent constraints including sequence discreteness, context length, structural coupling, and physical or thermodynamic requirements from architecture-dependent advantages that reflect the current state of the field. Current studies suggest that long-context models are particularly useful for genome-scale representation and sequence modeling, whereas structure-aware diffusion, flow-based, and inverse-folding approaches provide better frameworks for geometry-constrained RNA and protein design. This perspective provides a critical framework for understanding the present capabilities, limitations, and convergence of generative approaches toward reliable and experimentally grounded biological design.']

title: Upcycling Vegetable Waste Into Functional Food Ingredients via Synergistic Microbial Engineering and Artificial Intelligence.
authors: Jiajin Sun; Dongbo Ma; Qingwei Meng; Chongpeng Bi; Jianping Li; Anshan Shan
journal: Comprehensive reviews in food science and food safety
abstract: ['The escalating generation of global vegetable waste represents a critical loss of bioactive resources, necessitating a paradigm shift from passive disposal to active nutrient upcycling. However, the industrial conversion of this heterogeneous biomass into standardized functional food ingredients is currently impeded by significant techno-economic barriers, primarily structural recalcitrance, compositional inconsistency, and the presence of toxic fermentation inhibitors. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of the synergistic application of microbial engineering and artificial intelligence (AI) to resolve these bioprocessing bottlenecks within a food-to-food closed-loop framework (as shown in the graphical abstract). We evaluate recent advances in engineering food-grade microbial chassis (e.g., Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Escherichia coli) to enhance lignocellulose degradation and stress tolerance. Concurrently, we examine the integration of AI across the entire value chain, covering deep learning-based rational enzyme design, genome-scale metabolic modeling, and intelligent process control for precision fermentation. Current evidence demonstrates that the hardware-software coupling of engineered strains and AI algorithms significantly enhances conversion efficiency and process robustness. Key findings highlight that AI-driven Design-Build-Test-Learn cycles facilitate the de novo creation of enzymes with superior kinetics and strains with adaptive stress response capabilities against toxins. Moreover, dynamic digital twin models effectively mitigate the impact of substrate variability, ensuring the batch-to-batch consistency required for food applications. We conclude that this data-driven synergistic paradigm is pivotal for establishing a resilient circular bioeconomy, enabling the reliable bioconversion of waste into high-value single-cell proteins, natural flavor additives, and sustainable packaging materials.']

title: <sup>68</sup>Ga-Labeled Dimeric Cyclic Peptide for Nectin-4-Targeted PET Imaging: From Preclinical Evaluation to First-in-Human Imaging in Breast Cancer.
authors: Shushan Ge; Jihui Li; Jinyu Shi; Tongtong Jia; Dingding Ai; Junpeng Li; Shibiao Sang; Jing Lan; Bin Zhang; Shengming Deng
journal: Journal of nuclear medicine : official publication, Society of Nuclear Medicine
abstract: ['Nectin-4 is an attractive target for molecular imaging and targeted therapy because of its overexpression in multiple malignancies. We developed a nectin cell adhesion molecule 4 (nectin-4)-targeted 68Ga-labeled dimeric cyclic peptide PET tracer, [68Ga]Ga-TDN1, for noninvasive imaging of nectin-4 expression. Methods: TDN1 was generated by click chemistry to conjugate 2 nectin-4-binding bicyclic peptides and was radiolabeled with 68Ga. Binding affinity was assessed by surface plasmon resonance. Target specificity and tumor-targeting ability were evaluated by cell uptake, blocking, small-animal PET/CT, and biodistribution studies in nectin-4-positive and nectin-4-negative tumor models. [68Ga]Ga-TDN1 was further compared with [68Ga]Ga-N188 in preclinical models. After preclinical evaluation, [68Ga]Ga-TDN1 PET/CT was investigated in a pilot first-in-human study in 6 patients with breast cancer and directly compared with [18F]FDG PET/CT. Results: TDN1 showed high affinity for nectin-4 (K D = 1.92 × 10-10 M). In preclinical studies, [68Ga]Ga-TDN1 showed specific uptake in nectin-4-positive cells and tumors, low uptake in nectin-4-negative models, and marked reduction in uptake under blocking conditions. Compared with [68Ga]Ga-N188, [68Ga]Ga-TDN1 showed higher tumor uptake and longer retention across multiple nectin-4-positive xenografts. In the pilot clinical study, [68Ga]Ga-TDN1 was well-tolerated and showed favorable biodistribution and dosimetry. [68Ga]Ga-TDN1 PET/CT revealed imaging performance comparable to that of [18F]FDG PET/CT for primary tumors and most nodal metastases and demonstrated higher uptake and improved lesion detection in bone and liver metastases in selected patients. [68Ga]Ga-TDN1 was a clinically translatable nectin-4-targeted PET tracer with high affinity, favorable pharmacokinetics, and specific tumor uptake. Preclinical and pilot clinical results supported further clinical evaluation of [68Ga]Ga-TDN1 for noninvasive imaging of nectin-4 expression, particularly for assessment of metastatic disease.']

title: Omics-guided understanding of nonthermal plasma seed treatment: from surface modification to germination and stress resilience.
authors: Kainat Gul; Sohail Mumtaz
abstract: ['This review links plasma-induced seed-surface modification and redox signaling with emerging multi-omics responses associated with germination and stress resilience, while emphasizing that a unified causal sequence remains unproven. Nonthermal plasma (NTP) seed treatment has emerged as a promising chemical-free strategy for improving germination, seedling establishment, and stress resilience. Despite the expansion of plasma agriculture, reviews have largely focused on plasma engineering, individual physiological responses, or descriptive summaries of agronomic outcomes, leaving the mechanistic continuum linking plasma-derived signals to molecular reprogramming and stress-resilient phenotypes fragmented. Here, we provide an omics-guided and systems-level synthesis of NTP seed treatment by integrating evidence from both direct plasma treatment and plasma-activated water within a unified conceptual framework. We evaluate NTP-generated reactive species, ultraviolet photons, and transient electric fields as upstream signals contributing to biological responses across multiple organizational levels, while recognizing that their relative contributions and causal ordering remain unresolved. We synthesize evidence linking plasma exposure with seed-surface remodeling, redox and hormonal signaling, and transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and locus-specific epigenetic responses. However, these layers have largely been examined across different species, tissues, developmental stages, and experimental systems and therefore do not establish a unified causal chain for germination or stress adaptation. By integrating surface-level effects with molecular evidence, this review frames NTP seed treatment as a dose-dependent redox intervention that may transiently reconfigure conserved signaling networks, while direct cross-scale mechanistic validation remains limited. Finally, we identify critical challenges, including the lack of standardized plasma dosimetry, source variability, and limited cross-scale mechanistic integration, and propose a roadmap toward precision plasma agriculture through multi-omics-guided biomarker discovery, real-time plasma diagnostics, artificial intelligence-assisted optimization, and customized plasma treatments aimed at improving crop establishment and stress resilience.']

title: Development of proteome-derived cyclic peptide libraries via ortho-phthalaldehyde-assisted cyclization.

abstract: ['Cyclic peptides possess unique structural features and binding capabilities that make them attractive scaffolds for molecular recognition. title: Omics-guided understanding of nonthermal plasma seed treatment: from surface modification to germination and stress resilience.
authors: Kainat Gul; Sohail Mumtaz
abstract: ['This review links plasma-induced seed-surface modification and redox signaling with emerging multi-omics responses associated with germination and stress resilience, while emphasizing that a unified causal sequence remains unproven. By integrating surface-level effects with molecular evidence, this review frames NTP seed treatment as a dose-dependent redox intervention that may transiently reconfigure conserved signaling networks, while direct cross-scale mechanistic validation remains limited. Finally, we identify critical challenges, including the lack of standardized plasma dosimetry, source variability, and limited cross-scale mechanistic integration, and propose a roadmap toward precision plasma agriculture through multi-omics-guided biomarker discovery, real-time plasma diagnostics, artificial intelligence-assisted optimization, and customized plasma treatments aimed at improving crop establishment and stress resilience.']

title: Invisible Infrastructure at Risk: Funding Crises Threaten Global Bioscience Research.
authors: Valerie Wood; Elspeth A Bruford; Steven J Marygold; Valerie B O'Donnell; Katja Röper; Jamie A Davies; Christine Orengo; Paul Nurse; Neil Hall
abstract: ['Modern biology depends on invisible infrastructure that is essential yet precariously funded. Millions of biological observations are interpreted through resources that sit beneath routine scientific practice, largely unseen in everyday research. Every experiment, genome analysis, AI model, and clinical interpretation relies on these biological knowledgebases, which most researchers rarely notice until they disappear. That infrastructure is now under threat. Across the world, the biological databases that underpin modern research, built over decades of public and charitable investment, face severe and increasing financial instability. This crisis arrives at a particularly damaging moment: many governments have identified life sciences as a strategic growth sector and are investing heavily in genomics, AI-enabled drug discovery, and precision medicine. Yet every one of these ambitions ultimately depends on curated biological data resources reliant on emergency bridge grants, donations, staff secondments, and ad hoc rescue efforts.']

title: AI-enabled fungal biomanufacturing: from genome mining to the artificial intelligence virtual cell.
authors: Zhixuan Wang; Xuanye Chen; Shuying Gu; Peiqi Wang; Jingen Li; Shuang Zhou; Shouyue Zhang
abstract: ['Fungi are important chassis organisms for sustainable biomanufacturing owing to their strong secretion capacity, metabolic diversity, and adaptability to industrial processes. Driven by the rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI), computational approaches that enable machines to learn patterns from data and make predictions, together with omics technologies and synthetic biology, data- and model-driven strategies are increasingly reshaping fungal cell factory design and optimization. This review summarizes recent advances in AI-enabled fungal biomanufacturing, covering AI-assisted genome mining, enzyme and pathway analysis, genome editing, metabolic network modeling, and intelligent fermentation control. The review further highlights the emerging concept of the artificial intelligence virtual cell (AIVC), which integrates multi-omics data, mechanistic modeling, and machine learning-based approaches into a unified multiscale framework for simulating dynamic cellular behaviors. The technical foundations and potential applications of AIVC in fungal metabolic engineering, drug discovery, agriculture, and environmental biotechnology are reviewed. Finally, key challenges-data quality and standardization, cross-scale model integration and interpretability, and the gap between in silico prediction and experimental validation-are highlighted. This review provides a systematic perspective on the role of AI and virtual cell technologies in advancing next generation fungal biotechnology.']

title: Deep generative models in biological sequence and structure analysis and design.
authors: Fahimeh Palizban; Mohammadmahdi Sarbishegi; Huiqi Qu; Amir Hossein Saeidian; Mahya Mehrmohamadi; Joseph Glessner; Hakon Hakonarson
abstract: ['Deep generative models have transformed biological sequence modeling from predictive analysis toward increasingly controllable design. Early biological applications of Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) established latent representation learning and sequence synthesis, while recent advances in transformer-based language models, discrete diffusion, flow-matching, and multimodal generative frameworks have substantially expanded the scope of biological design. This review examines generative models for DNA, RNA, and protein sequence design, emphasizing how different model classes represent biological constraints, operate over discrete and continuous spaces, and integrate sequence, structure, and function. We compare VAEs, GANs, autoregressive and masked language models, diffusion models, and flow-based approaches across genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics, with particular attention to controllability, long-range dependency modeling, structural grounding, generalization, and experimental utility. We further examine evaluation strategies, out-of-distribution generalization, and closed-loop design-build-test-learn workflows that connect in silico generation with empirical validation. We distinguish fundamental modality-dependent constraints including sequence discreteness, context length, structural coupling, and physical or thermodynamic requirements from architecture-dependent advantages that reflect the current state of the field. Current studies suggest that long-context models are particularly useful for genome-scale representation and sequence modeling, whereas structure-aware diffusion, flow-based, and inverse-folding approaches provide better frameworks for geometry-constrained RNA and protein design. This perspective provides a critical framework for understanding the present capabilities, limitations, and convergence of generative approaches toward reliable and experimentally grounded biological design.']

title: Upcycling Vegetable Waste Into Functional Food Ingredients via Synergistic Microbial Engineering and Artificial Intelligence.
authors: Jiajin Sun; Dongbo Ma; Qingwei Meng; Chongpeng Bi; Jianping Li; Anshan Shan
journal: Comprehensive reviews in food science and food safety
abstract: ['The escalating generation of global vegetable waste represents a critical loss of bioactive resources, necessitating a paradigm shift from passive disposal to active nutrient upcycling. However, the industrial conversion of this heterogeneous biomass into standardized functional food ingredients is currently impeded by significant techno-economic barriers, primarily structural recalcitrance, compositional inconsistency, and the presence of toxic fermentation inhibitors. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of the synergistic application of microbial engineering and artificial intelligence (AI) to resolve these bioprocessing bottlenecks within a food-to-food closed-loop framework (as shown in the graphical abstract). We evaluate recent advances in engineering food-grade microbial chassis (e.g., Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Escherichia coli) to enhance lignocellulose degradation and stress tolerance. Concurrently, we examine the integration of AI across the entire value chain, covering deep learning-based rational enzyme design, genome-scale metabolic modeling, and intelligent process control for precision fermentation. Current evidence demonstrates that the hardware-software coupling of engineered strains and AI algorithms significantly enhances conversion efficiency and process robustness. Key findings highlight that AI-driven Design-Build-Test-Learn cycles facilitate the de novo creation of enzymes with superior kinetics and strains with adaptive stress response capabilities against toxins. Moreover, dynamic digital twin models effectively mitigate the impact of substrate variability, ensuring the batch-to-batch consistency required for food applications. We conclude that this data-driven synergistic paradigm is pivotal for establishing a resilient circular bioeconomy, enabling the reliable bioconversion of waste into high-value single-cell proteins, natural flavor additives, and sustainable packaging materials.']

title: <sup>68</sup>Ga-Labeled Dimeric Cyclic Peptide for Nectin-4-Targeted PET Imaging: From Preclinical Evaluation to First-in-Human Imaging in Breast Cancer.
authors: Shushan Ge; Jihui Li; Jinyu Shi; Tongtong Jia; Dingding Ai; Junpeng Li; Shibiao Sang; Jing Lan; Bin Zhang; Shengming Deng
journal: Journal of nuclear medicine : official publication, Society of Nuclear Medicine
abstract: ['Nectin-4 is an attractive target for molecular imaging and targeted therapy because of its overexpression in multiple malignancies. We developed a nectin cell adhesion molecule 4 (nectin-4)-targeted 68Ga-labeled dimeric cyclic peptide PET tracer, [68Ga]Ga-TDN1, for noninvasive imaging of nectin-4 expression. Methods: TDN1 was generated by click chemistry to conjugate 2 nectin-4-binding bicyclic peptides and was radiolabeled with 68Ga. Binding affinity was assessed by surface plasmon resonance. Target specificity and tumor-targeting ability were evaluated by cell uptake, blocking, small-animal PET/CT, and biodistribution studies in nectin-4-positive and nectin-4-negative tumor models. [68Ga]Ga-TDN1 was further compared with [68Ga]Ga-N188 in preclinical models. After preclinical evaluation, [68Ga]Ga-TDN1 PET/CT was investigated in a pilot first-in-human study in 6 patients with breast cancer and directly compared with [18F]FDG PET/CT. Results: TDN1 showed high affinity for nectin-4 (K D = 1.92 × 10-10 M). In preclinical studies, [68Ga]Ga-TDN1 showed specific uptake in nectin-4-positive cells and tumors, low uptake in nectin-4-negative models, and marked reduction in uptake under blocking conditions. Compared with [68Ga]Ga-N188, [68Ga]Ga-TDN1 showed higher tumor uptake and longer retention across multiple nectin-4-positive xenografts. In the pilot clinical study, [68Ga]Ga-TDN1 was well-tolerated and showed favorable biodistribution and dosimetry. [68Ga]Ga-TDN1 PET/CT revealed imaging performance comparable to that of [18F]FDG PET/CT for primary tumors and most nodal metastases and demonstrated higher uptake and improved lesion detection in bone and liver metastases in selected patients. [68Ga]Ga-TDN1 was a clinically translatable nectin-4-targeted PET tracer with high affinity, favorable pharmacokinetics, and specific tumor uptake. Preclinical and pilot clinical results supported further clinical evaluation of [68Ga]Ga-TDN1 for noninvasive imaging of nectin-4 expression, particularly for assessment of metastatic disease.']

title: Development of proteome-derived cyclic peptide libraries via ortho-phthalaldehyde-assisted cyclization.
authors: Ying Wei; Kangze Feng; Wenxuan Hou; Xiaolin Tian; Yuanyuan Xue; Wenhao Zhang; Haiteng Deng
abstract: ['Cyclic peptides possess unique structural features and binding capabilities that make them attractive scaffolds for molecular recognition. However, strategies for generating functionally diverse libraries directly from natural proteomes remain comparatively underdeveloped. Here, we present a proteome-informed approach for constructing cyclic peptide libraries by integrating cysteine-enrichment protocols with ortho-phthalaldehyde (OPA)-mediated macrocyclization. This method enables direct library generation from proteome digests and is compatible with liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS)-based annotation and downstream functional screening. We systematically identify key parameters governing OPA-mediated cyclization topology and develop a rule-based pipeline for automated library annotation of OPA-cyclized peptides. Applying this strategy, we generate a library of over 15,000 unique cyclic peptides and perform target-specific screening against human IgG. This yielded cyclic peptide binder candidates, including one lead peptide showing cyclization-dependent IgG-binding potential. Our study establishes an OPA-enabled, proteome-informed workflow for cyclic peptide library construction and annotation.']

title: Bioinformatics-driven discovery of bioactive natural peptides from cyanobacterial genomes.
authors: Maryam Tabarzad; Mohadeseh Heidari; Bita Norouzi
abstract: ['Cyanobacteria, as photosynthetic microorganisms, are emerging as a significant source of bioactive peptides with tremendous therapeutic potential against cancer, infections, and inflammatory diseases. Recent studies have highlighted that cyanobacteria produce a wide variety of non-ribosomal peptides (NRPs), polyketides (PKs), hybrids of NRPs and PKs, as well as ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs). They are produced through modular biosynthetic pathways that involve NRPS, PKS, and hybrid systems, along with extensive enzymatic modifications, resulting in large families of related compounds. The current review highlights advanced bioinformatics techniques that improve our capacity to discover and characterize natural biomaterials from cyanobacterial genomes, focusing on both ribosomally and non-ribosomally synthesized peptides. Advanced genome mining tools, such as antiSMASH and PRISM, alongside specialized databases like the Cyanobacterial Metabolomics Database (CyanoMetDB), are revolutionizing our understanding of biosynthetic gene clusters and biochemical scaffold prediction. Furthermore, integrating genomics with transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics is crucial for linking orphan gene clusters to their corresponding products and prioritizing underexplored pathways for validation. While significant advancements have been made, challenges remain in accurate structure prediction and functional annotation. Nevertheless, the application of bioinformatics and artificial intelligence is transforming cyanobacterial natural product discovery, unveiling a largely untapped reservoir of peptide diversity with strong implications for drug discovery and biotechnology. Realizing this potential could result in innovative solutions to critical medical and environmental challenges.']

title: Omics-guided understanding of nonthermal plasma seed treatment: from surface modification to germination and stress resilience.
authors: Kainat Gul; Sohail Mumtaz
abstract: ['This review links plasma-induced seed-surface modification and redox signaling with emerging multi-omics responses associated with germination and stress resilience, while emphasizing that a unified causal sequence remains unproven. Nonthermal plasma (NTP) seed treatment has emerged as a promising chemical-free strategy for improving germination, seedling establishment, and stress resilience. Despite the expansion of plasma agriculture, reviews have largely focused on plasma engineering, individual physiological responses, or descriptive summaries of agronomic outcomes, leaving the mechanistic continuum linking plasma-derived signals to molecular reprogramming and stress-resilient phenotypes fragmented. Here, we provide an omics-guided and systems-level synthesis of NTP seed treatment by integrating evidence from both direct plasma treatment and plasma-activated water within a unified conceptual framework. We evaluate NTP-generated reactive species, ultraviolet photons, and transient electric fields as upstream signals contributing to biological responses across multiple organizational levels, while recognizing that their relative contributions and causal ordering remain unresolved. We synthesize evidence linking plasma exposure with seed-surface remodeling, redox and hormonal signaling, and transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and locus-specific epigenetic responses. However, these layers have largely been examined across different species, tissues, developmental stages, and experimental systems and therefore do not establish a unified causal chain for germination or stress adaptation. By integrating surface-level effects with molecular evidence, this review frames NTP seed treatment as a dose-dependent redox intervention that may transiently reconfigure conserved signaling networks, while direct cross-scale mechanistic validation remains limited. Finally, we identify critical challenges, including the lack of standardized plasma dosimetry, source variability, and limited cross-scale mechanistic integration, and propose a roadmap toward precision plasma agriculture through multi-omics-guided biomarker discovery, real-time plasma diagnostics, artificial intelligence-assisted optimization, and customized plasma treatments aimed at improving crop establishment and stress resilience.']

title: Gene-Driven Precision Medicine: Enhancing Biomarker Identification for Personalized Therapy.
authors: Mohamed Abbas; Abdallah Saleh; Hashim Elshafie; Mohamad Yahya H Al-Shamri; Suresh Babu Changalasetty; Azath Mubarakali
abstract: ['Transformative advances in biomarker science are reshaping the landscape of precision medicine, offering powerful tools for early disease detection, accurate prognostication, and individualized therapeutic design. This review synthesizes recent progress in biomarker discovery, classification, and clinical application across multiple medical domains, emphasizing their pivotal role in enhancing diagnostic precision and personalizing treatment strategies. Central to these advances is the integration of next-generation sequencing, advanced mass spectrometry, artificial intelligence, and multi-omics technologies, which collectively strengthen biomarker reliability and reproducibility. The review also explores the contributions of non-coding RNAs, tumor microenvironment dynamics, and immune-inflammatory pathways in constructing disease-specific biomarker profiles. In fields such as oncology, neurology, and infectious diseases, biomarker-driven approaches are transforming drug development and clinical decision-making. However, challenges such as biological variability, lack of standardization, and ethical concerns necessitate coordinated, multidisciplinary solutions. Emerging innovations, including machine learning-driven analytics, single-cell technologies, and wearable biosensors, signal a shift toward more dynamic diagnostics and adaptive interventions. By charting the current and emerging biomarker landscape, this review underscores the shift toward patient-centric care models. It concludes by highlighting the importance of cross-sector collaboration to accelerate the clinical translation of biomarker innovations, ultimately advancing health equity and improving global healthcare outcomes.']

title: Deep generative models in biological sequence and structure analysis and design.
authors: Fahimeh Palizban; Mohammadmahdi Sarbishegi; Huiqi Qu; Amir Hossein Saeidian; Mahya Mehrmohamadi; Joseph Glessner; Hakon Hakonarson
abstract: ['Deep generative models have transformed biological sequence modeling from predictive analysis toward increasingly controllable design. Early biological applications of Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) established latent representation learning and sequence synthesis, while recent advances in transformer-based language models, discrete diffusion, flow-matching, and multimodal generative frameworks have substantially expanded the scope of biological design. This review examines generative models for DNA, RNA, and protein sequence design, emphasizing how different model classes represent biological constraints, operate over discrete and continuous spaces, and integrate sequence, structure, and function. We compare VAEs, GANs, autoregressive and masked language models, diffusion models, and flow-based approaches across genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics, with particular attention to controllability, long-range dependency modeling, structural grounding, generalization, and experimental utility. We further examine evaluation strategies, out-of-distribution generalization, and closed-loop design-build-test-learn workflows that connect in silico generation with empirical validation. We distinguish fundamental modality-dependent constraints including sequence discreteness, context length, structural coupling, and physical or thermodynamic requirements from architecture-dependent advantages that reflect the current state of the field. Current studies suggest that long-context models are particularly useful for genome-scale representation and sequence modeling, whereas structure-aware diffusion, flow-based, and inverse-folding approaches provide better frameworks for geometry-constrained RNA and protein design. This perspective provides a critical framework for understanding the present capabilities, limitations, and convergence of generative approaches toward reliable and experimentally grounded biological design.']

title: Artificial intelligence in central nervous system autoimmune diseases: from clinical decision support to mechanistic discovery and translation.
authors: Zijian Cao; Pei Zheng; Zhihui Qi; Yang Yao; Donglin Xie; Yazi He; Shenghua Zong; Zongjiu Zhang; Fu-Dong Shi
abstract: ['Central nervous system (CNS) autoimmune diseases, including multiple sclerosis (MS), neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD), autoimmune encephalitis (AE), and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD), remain difficult to diagnose, stratify, and treat because clinical phenotypes overlap, biomarkers are imperfect, and the disease course requires longitudinal observation. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being evaluated to integrate clinical, imaging, immunological, and molecular data for decision-making in neuroimmunology. Clinical applications include automated neuroimaging analysis, differential diagnosis, disease classification, relapse prediction, prognostic stratification, and risk-informed care planning. Evidence is unevenly distributed: MS has the largest body of published work, particularly in neuroimaging, whereas studies in NMOSD, AE, and MOGAD are smaller, more heterogeneous, and often lack external validation. Computational approaches are also being applied to multi-omics, single-cell and spatial data, molecular target prioritisation, drug repositioning, trial enrichment, digital biomarkers, federated learning, and longitudinal modelling; however, these applications generally provide association, prioritisation, or hypothesis-generating evidence rather than validated therapeutic benefit. This Review maps reported applications, evidence patterns, and methodological and implementation needs rather than ranking translational maturity or implying established clinical benefit.']

title: AI in Neuro-Oncology: An Overarching Review.
authors: Carla Pitarch-Abaigar; Philipp Lohmann; Patrick Aloy; Fatima Al-Shahrour; Omar Arnaout; Wenya Linda Bi; Norbert Galldiks; Jason T Huse; Philipp Karschnia; MacLean P Nasrallah; Areeba Patel; Rifaquat Rahman; Felix Sahm; Timothy R Smith; Joerg-Christian Tonn; Renato Umeton; Manuel Valiente; Mark Zarella; Raymond Y Huang; Spyridon Bakas
abstract: ['Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied across neuro-oncology domains to analyze complex, high-dimensional, multimodal data. Despite major advances in the biological understanding and classification of CNS tumors, clinical outcomes for many of them remain poor, reflecting intra- and inter-tumor heterogeneity and limitations of conventional reductionist approaches. AI offers a paradigm shift to capture this heterogeneity and provide quantitative, reproducible diagnostic, predictive, and prognostic insights. This article describes a joint effort across the Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology (RANO) working groups to provide an overarching review of the AI use across six key domains of neuro-oncology: neuroimaging, neuropathology, laboratory medicine, neurosurgery, drug discovery, and clinical trials. Applications closest to clinical use include imaging segmentation and quantification, AI-assisted image reconstruction, DNA methylation-based classification, and workflow optimization. title: Upcycling Vegetable Waste Into Functional Food Ingredients via Synergistic Microbial Engineering and Artificial Intelligence.
authors: Jiajin Sun; Dongbo Ma; Qingwei Meng; Chongpeng Bi; Jianping Li; Anshan Shan
journal: Comprehensive reviews in food science and food safety
abstract: ['The escalating generation of global vegetable waste represents a critical loss of bioactive resources, necessitating a paradigm shift from passive disposal to active nutrient upcycling. title: <sup>68</sup>Ga-Labeled Dimeric Cyclic Peptide for Nectin-4-Targeted PET Imaging: From Preclinical Evaluation to First-in-Human Imaging in Breast Cancer.

abstract: ['Nectin-4 is an attractive target for molecular imaging and targeted therapy because of its overexpression in multiple malignancies. [68Ga]Ga-TDN1 was further compared with [68Ga]Ga-N188 in preclinical models. After preclinical evaluation, [68Ga]Ga-TDN1 PET/CT was investigated in a pilot first-in-human study in 6 patients with breast cancer and directly compared with [18F]FDG PET/CT. Results: TDN1 showed high affinity for nectin-4 (K D = 1.92 × 10-10 M). In preclinical studies, [68Ga]Ga-TDN1 showed specific uptake in nectin-4-positive cells and tumors, low uptake in nectin-4-negative models, and marked reduction in uptake under blocking conditions. title: Development of proteome-derived cyclic peptide libraries via ortho-phthalaldehyde-assisted cyclization.
authors: Ying Wei; Kangze Feng; Wenxuan Hou; Xiaolin Tian; Yuanyuan Xue; Wenhao Zhang; Haiteng Deng
abstract: ['Cyclic peptides possess unique structural features and binding capabilities that make them attractive scaffolds for molecular recognition. However, strategies for generating functionally diverse libraries directly from natural proteomes remain comparatively underdeveloped. Here, we present a proteome-informed approach for constructing cyclic peptide libraries by integrating cysteine-enrichment protocols with ortho-phthalaldehyde (OPA)-mediated macrocyclization. title: Artificial intelligence in central nervous system autoimmune diseases: from clinical decision support to mechanistic discovery and translation.
authors: Zijian Cao; Pei Zheng; Zhihui Qi; Yang Yao; Donglin Xie; Yazi He; Shenghua Zong; Zongjiu Zhang; Fu-Dong Shi
abstract: ['Central nervous system (CNS) autoimmune diseases, including multiple sclerosis (MS), neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD), autoimmune encephalitis (AE), and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD), remain difficult to diagnose, stratify, and treat because clinical phenotypes overlap, biomarkers are imperfect, and the disease course requires longitudinal observation. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being evaluated to integrate clinical, imaging, immunological, and molecular data for decision-making in neuroimmunology. Clinical applications include automated neuroimaging analysis, differential diagnosis, disease classification, relapse prediction, prognostic stratification, and risk-informed care planning. Evidence is unevenly distributed: MS has the largest body of published work, particularly in neuroimaging, whereas studies in NMOSD, AE, and MOGAD are smaller, more heterogeneous, and often lack external validation. Computational approaches are also being applied to multi-omics, single-cell and spatial data, molecular target prioritisation, drug repositioning, trial enrichment, digital biomarkers, federated learning, and longitudinal modelling; however, these applications generally provide association, prioritisation, or hypothesis-generating evidence rather than validated therapeutic benefit. This Review maps reported applications, evidence patterns, and methodological and implementation needs rather than ranking translational maturity or implying established clinical benefit.']

title: Bioinformatics-driven discovery of bioactive natural peptides from cyanobacterial genomes.
authors: Maryam Tabarzad; Mohadeseh Heidari; Bita Norouzi
abstract: ['Cyanobacteria, as photosynthetic microorganisms, are emerging as a significant source of bioactive peptides with tremendous therapeutic potential against cancer, infections, and inflammatory diseases. Recent studies have highlighted that cyanobacteria produce a wide variety of non-ribosomal peptides (NRPs), polyketides (PKs), hybrids of NRPs and PKs, as well as ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs). They are produced through modular biosynthetic pathways that involve NRPS, PKS, and hybrid systems, along with extensive enzymatic modifications, resulting in large families of related compounds. The current review highlights advanced bioinformatics techniques that improve our capacity to discover and characterize natural biomaterials from cyanobacterial genomes, focusing on both ribosomally and non-ribosomally synthesized peptides. Advanced genome mining tools, such as antiSMASH and PRISM, alongside specialized databases like the Cyanobacterial Metabolomics Database (CyanoMetDB), are revolutionizing our understanding of biosynthetic gene clusters and biochemical scaffold prediction. Furthermore, integrating genomics with transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics is crucial for linking orphan gene clusters to their corresponding products and prioritizing underexplored pathways for validation. While significant advancements have been made, challenges remain in accurate structure prediction and functional annotation. Nevertheless, the application of bioinformatics and artificial intelligence is transforming cyanobacterial natural product discovery, unveiling a largely untapped reservoir of peptide diversity with strong implications for drug discovery and biotechnology. Realizing this potential could result in innovative solutions to critical medical and environmental challenges.']

title: AI in Neuro-Oncology: An Overarching Review.
authors: Carla Pitarch-Abaigar; Philipp Lohmann; Patrick Aloy; Fatima Al-Shahrour; Omar Arnaout; Wenya Linda Bi; Norbert Galldiks; Jason T Huse; Philipp Karschnia; MacLean P Nasrallah; Areeba Patel; Rifaquat Rahman; Felix Sahm; Timothy R Smith; Joerg-Christian Tonn; Renato Umeton; Manuel Valiente; Mark Zarella; Raymond Y Huang; Spyridon Bakas
abstract: ['Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied across neuro-oncology domains to analyze complex, high-dimensional, multimodal data. Despite major advances in the biological understanding and classification of CNS tumors, clinical outcomes for many of them remain poor, reflecting intra- and inter-tumor heterogeneity and limitations of conventional reductionist approaches. AI offers a paradigm shift to capture this heterogeneity and provide quantitative, reproducible diagnostic, predictive, and prognostic insights. This article describes a joint effort across the Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology (RANO) working groups to provide an overarching review of the AI use across six key domains of neuro-oncology: neuroimaging, neuropathology, laboratory medicine, neurosurgery, drug discovery, and clinical trials. Applications closest to clinical use include imaging segmentation and quantification, AI-assisted image reconstruction, DNA methylation-based classification, and workflow optimization. Radiogenomics, WSI-based molecular prediction, AI-guided surgical targeting, liquid biopsy interpretation, AI-guided drug discovery, digital twins, and in silico trials remain promising but require stronger prospective validation. Key challenges include limited availability of large diverse datasets, variability in data acquisition and reference standards, and limited external validation. This review provides a unifying framework for understanding the role of AI across neuro-oncology and highlights key considerations for its responsible implementation, emphasizing standardization, reproducibility, multi-institutional validation, and human oversight.']

title: Multi-objective antibody design and optimization using machine learning.
authors: Yun-Huai Kuo; Chloe N Brown; Ece Akin; Yunxuan Xie; Peter M Tessier
abstract: ['Antibodies, ranging from conventional immunoglobulins to single-domain and bispecific antibodies, are developed for a wide spectrum of therapeutic and diagnostic applications. However, lead antibodies are commonly engineered to optimize one or more key properties, including affinity, specificity, polyreactivity, stability, aggregation, and immunogenicity, and tradeoffs among these attributes frequently hinder the development of variants suitable for clinical use. Furthermore, identifying lead candidates with desirable properties typically requires multiple rounds of experimental screening and evaluation, particularly when targeting pre-selected epitopes or challenging, high-value targets such as G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), ion channels, and multipass membrane proteins. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods can streamline experimental screening and antibody generation methods. In this Review, we discuss both computational multi-objective optimization of existing antibodies and de novo antibody design. The application of AI/ML methods has the potential to overcome current bottlenecks in antibody development and accelerate the generation of improved therapeutics for human health.']

title: Artificial Intelligence in Chronic Rhinosinusitis: From Molecular Profiling to Personalized Clinical Management-A Systematic Review.
authors: Chi-Sheng Huang; Duen-Lii Hsieh; Jin-Yu Lin; Maysayawan Sreesawat; Te-Huei Yeh; Chih-Feng Lin
abstract: ['Chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) is a heterogeneous inflammatory disease imposing a substantial health and economic burden. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool to address CRS complexity in both clinical and research settings. We conducted a systematic review following PRISMA guidelines, searching PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase for peer-reviewed articles utilizing machine learning, deep learning, and natural language processing, with a focus on molecular-level or immunologic mechanisms in CRS. Thirty-one studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. Our results demonstrate that while AI-driven analysis helps stratify patient endotypes, the identified schemes exhibit substantial heterogeneity in cluster numbers and features, raising concerns about their reproducibility. AI applications also included histopathological image interpretation, drug discovery, biologic therapy selection, and prognostic modeling to evaluate revision surgery risks and olfactory dysfunction. However, using the PROBAST+AI framework, we found that 87.1% of the assessed studies carry a high overall risk of bias, mainly due to the reliance on apparent performance or internal validation and limited independent evaluation of model performance, indicating that many reported performance estimates may be optimistic. title: <sup>68</sup>Ga-Labeled Dimeric Cyclic Peptide for Nectin-4-Targeted PET Imaging: From Preclinical Evaluation to First-in-Human Imaging in Breast Cancer.

abstract: ['Nectin-4 is an attractive target for molecular imaging and targeted therapy because of its overexpression in multiple malignancies. title: Artificial intelligence in central nervous system autoimmune diseases: from clinical decision support to mechanistic discovery and translation.
authors: Zijian Cao; Pei Zheng; Zhihui Qi; Yang Yao; Donglin Xie; Yazi He; Shenghua Zong; Zongjiu Zhang; Fu-Dong Shi
abstract: ['Central nervous system (CNS) autoimmune diseases, including multiple sclerosis (MS), neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD), autoimmune encephalitis (AE), and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD), remain difficult to diagnose, stratify, and treat because clinical phenotypes overlap, biomarkers are imperfect, and the disease course requires longitudinal observation. Clinical applications include automated neuroimaging analysis, differential diagnosis, disease classification, relapse prediction, prognostic stratification, and risk-informed care planning. Evidence is unevenly distributed: MS has the largest body of published work, particularly in neuroimaging, whereas studies in NMOSD, AE, and MOGAD are smaller, more heterogeneous, and often lack external validation. Computational approaches are also being applied to multi-omics, single-cell and spatial data, molecular target prioritisation, drug repositioning, trial enrichment, digital biomarkers, federated learning, and longitudinal modelling; however, these applications generally provide association, prioritisation, or hypothesis-generating evidence rather than validated therapeutic benefit. This Review maps reported applications, evidence patterns, and methodological and implementation needs rather than ranking translational maturity or implying established clinical benefit.']

title: Artificial Intelligence in Chronic Rhinosinusitis: From Molecular Profiling to Personalized Clinical Management-A Systematic Review.
authors: Chi-Sheng Huang; Duen-Lii Hsieh; Jin-Yu Lin; Maysayawan Sreesawat; Te-Huei Yeh; Chih-Feng Lin
abstract: ['Chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) is a heterogeneous inflammatory disease imposing a substantial health and economic burden. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool to address CRS complexity in both clinical and research settings. We conducted a systematic review following PRISMA guidelines, searching PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase for peer-reviewed articles utilizing machine learning, deep learning, and natural language processing, with a focus on molecular-level or immunologic mechanisms in CRS. Thirty-one studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. Our results demonstrate that while AI-driven analysis helps stratify patient endotypes, the identified schemes exhibit substantial heterogeneity in cluster numbers and features, raising concerns about their reproducibility. AI applications also included histopathological image interpretation, drug discovery, biologic therapy selection, and prognostic modeling to evaluate revision surgery risks and olfactory dysfunction. However, using the PROBAST+AI framework, we found that 87.1% of the assessed studies carry a high overall risk of bias, mainly due to the reliance on apparent performance or internal validation and limited independent evaluation of model performance, indicating that many reported performance estimates may be optimistic. Future large-scale, multicenter collaborations integrating AI into clinical workflows will be essential to establish reliable and generalizable AI applications for personalized CRS management.']

title: Toxoplasmosis: Epidemiological Significance, Economic Burden, and Emerging Directions in Drug Discovery and Artificial Intelligence.
authors: Albert Fynn Aiduenu; Blessing Kwabena Gayi; Aboagye Kwarteng Dofuor; Susanna Awinsongya Anovunga; William Ekloh; Joseph Harold Nyarko Osei; Christopher Nii Laryea Tawiah-Mensah; Juliet Ama Mawusi Koudonu Seglah; Jennifer Afua Afrifa Yamoah; Angelina Akomea; Andy Asafu-Adjaye
abstract: ["Toxoplasmosis, a parasitic disease caused by Toxoplasma gondii, affects a wide range of warm-blooded hosts and remains most prevalent in tropical regions, with distribution shaped by climate, cultural practices, and environmental conditions. Clinical severity varies across susceptible populations, generating substantial economic burdens through medical costs and agricultural losses. Given this global health impact, a comprehensive, up-to-date understanding of the disease is essential. However, significant gaps persist. While diagnostic techniques and epidemiological surveillance have advanced considerably, treatment protocols have remained largely unchanged for decades, revealing a disconnect between diagnostic innovation and therapeutic progress. Moreover, existing literature lacks an integrative synthesis connecting these advances to their broader significance, leaving researchers without a unified framework for understanding where the field stands and where it should go next. To address these gaps, this narrative review draws on peer-reviewed literature and institutional reports across major biomedical databases, synthesizing findings descriptively and thematically rather than through statistical meta-analysis. It critically examines toxoplasmosis across several dimensions. It first considers geographical distribution and the cultural, environmental, and economic factors shaping its epidemiology. It then turns to the parasite's biochemical and molecular characteristics, using this foundation to evaluate persistent limitations in treatment and vaccine development, an area where progress has stalled. In response, the review explores emerging alternatives, including plant-based compounds, as avenues beyond conventional pharmacological strategies. Finally, it examines artificial intelligence as an underexplored but promising tool for improving diagnosis and treatment, an area with limited application to toxoplasmosis specifically. By consolidating these threads, this review clarifies not only what is known about toxoplasmosis but also where critical gaps in treatment innovation and integrative understanding continue to hinder effective prevention and control."]

title: Deep generative models in biological sequence and structure analysis and design.

abstract: ['Deep generative models have transformed biological sequence modeling from predictive analysis toward increasingly controllable design. title: Multi-objective antibody design and optimization using machine learning.
authors: Yun-Huai Kuo; Chloe N Brown; Ece Akin; Yunxuan Xie; Peter M Tessier
abstract: ['Antibodies, ranging from conventional immunoglobulins to single-domain and bispecific antibodies, are developed for a wide spectrum of therapeutic and diagnostic applications. title: <sup>68</sup>Ga-Labeled Dimeric Cyclic Peptide for Nectin-4-Targeted PET Imaging: From Preclinical Evaluation to First-in-Human Imaging in Breast Cancer.
authors: Shushan Ge; Jihui Li; Jinyu Shi; Tongtong Jia; Dingding Ai; Junpeng Li; Shibiao Sang; Jing Lan; Bin Zhang; Shengming Deng
journal: Journal of nuclear medicine : official publication, Society of Nuclear Medicine
abstract: ['Nectin-4 is an attractive target for molecular imaging and targeted therapy because of its overexpression in multiple malignancies. [68Ga]Ga-TDN1 was further compared with [68Ga]Ga-N188 in preclinical models. After preclinical evaluation, [68Ga]Ga-TDN1 PET/CT was investigated in a pilot first-in-human study in 6 patients with breast cancer and directly compared with [18F]FDG PET/CT. Results: TDN1 showed high affinity for nectin-4 (K D = 1.92 × 10-10 M). In the pilot clinical study, [68Ga]Ga-TDN1 was well-tolerated and showed favorable biodistribution and dosimetry. title: Toxoplasmosis: Epidemiological Significance, Economic Burden, and Emerging Directions in Drug Discovery and Artificial Intelligence.
authors: Albert Fynn Aiduenu; Blessing Kwabena Gayi; Aboagye Kwarteng Dofuor; Susanna Awinsongya Anovunga; William Ekloh; Joseph Harold Nyarko Osei; Christopher Nii Laryea Tawiah-Mensah; Juliet Ama Mawusi Koudonu Seglah; Jennifer Afua Afrifa Yamoah; Angelina Akomea; Andy Asafu-Adjaye
abstract: ["Toxoplasmosis, a parasitic disease caused by Toxoplasma gondii, affects a wide range of warm-blooded hosts and remains most prevalent in tropical regions, with distribution shaped by climate, cultural practices, and environmental conditions. Clinical severity varies across susceptible populations, generating substantial economic burdens through medical costs and agricultural losses. Given this global health impact, a comprehensive, up-to-date understanding of the disease is essential. However, significant gaps persist. While diagnostic techniques and epidemiological surveillance have advanced considerably, treatment protocols have remained largely unchanged for decades, revealing a disconnect between diagnostic innovation and therapeutic progress. Moreover, existing literature lacks an integrative synthesis connecting these advances to their broader significance, leaving researchers without a unified framework for understanding where the field stands and where it should go next. To address these gaps, this narrative review draws on peer-reviewed literature and institutional reports across major biomedical databases, synthesizing findings descriptively and thematically rather than through statistical meta-analysis. It critically examines toxoplasmosis across several dimensions. It first considers geographical distribution and the cultural, environmental, and economic factors shaping its epidemiology. It then turns to the parasite's biochemical and molecular characteristics, using this foundation to evaluate persistent limitations in treatment and vaccine development, an area where progress has stalled. In response, the review explores emerging alternatives, including plant-based compounds, as avenues beyond conventional pharmacological strategies. Finally, it examines artificial intelligence as an underexplored but promising tool for improving diagnosis and treatment, an area with limited application to toxoplasmosis specifically. By consolidating these threads, this review clarifies not only what is known about toxoplasmosis but also where critical gaps in treatment innovation and integrative understanding continue to hinder effective prevention and control."]

title: Artificial Intelligence in Chronic Rhinosinusitis: From Molecular Profiling to Personalized Clinical Management-A Systematic Review.
authors: Chi-Sheng Huang; Duen-Lii Hsieh; Jin-Yu Lin; Maysayawan Sreesawat; Te-Huei Yeh; Chih-Feng Lin
abstract: ['Chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) is a heterogeneous inflammatory disease imposing a substantial health and economic burden. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool to address CRS complexity in both clinical and research settings. We conducted a systematic review following PRISMA guidelines, searching PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase for peer-reviewed articles utilizing machine learning, deep learning, and natural language processing, with a focus on molecular-level or immunologic mechanisms in CRS. Thirty-one studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. Our results demonstrate that while AI-driven analysis helps stratify patient endotypes, the identified schemes exhibit substantial heterogeneity in cluster numbers and features, raising concerns about their reproducibility. AI applications also included histopathological image interpretation, drug discovery, biologic therapy selection, and prognostic modeling to evaluate revision surgery risks and olfactory dysfunction. However, using the PROBAST+AI framework, we found that 87.1% of the assessed studies carry a high overall risk of bias, mainly due to the reliance on apparent performance or internal validation and limited independent evaluation of model performance, indicating that many reported performance estimates may be optimistic. Future large-scale, multicenter collaborations integrating AI into clinical workflows will be essential to establish reliable and generalizable AI applications for personalized CRS management.']

title: Multi-objective antibody design and optimization using machine learning.
authors: Yun-Huai Kuo; Chloe N Brown; Ece Akin; Yunxuan Xie; Peter M Tessier
abstract: ['Antibodies, ranging from conventional immunoglobulins to single-domain and bispecific antibodies, are developed for a wide spectrum of therapeutic and diagnostic applications. title: <sup>68</sup>Ga-Labeled Dimeric Cyclic Peptide for Nectin-4-Targeted PET Imaging: From Preclinical Evaluation to First-in-Human Imaging in Breast Cancer.
authors: Shushan Ge; Jihui Li; Jinyu Shi; Tongtong Jia; Dingding Ai; Junpeng Li; Shibiao Sang; Jing Lan; Bin Zhang; Shengming Deng
journal: Journal of nuclear medicine : official publication, Society of Nuclear Medicine
abstract: ['Nectin-4 is an attractive target for molecular imaging and targeted therapy because of its overexpression in multiple malignancies. [68Ga]Ga-TDN1 was further compared with [68Ga]Ga-N188 in preclinical models. After preclinical evaluation, [68Ga]Ga-TDN1 PET/CT was investigated in a pilot first-in-human study in 6 patients with breast cancer and directly compared with [18F]FDG PET/CT. Results: TDN1 showed high affinity for nectin-4 (K D = 1.92 × 10-10 M). abstract: ['Peptide-functionalized gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) provide a model for decoding how the surface-bound secondary structure regulates nano-bio interactions.
