title: Advances in Somatostatin Receptor-Targeting Peptide Receptor Radionuclide Therapy for Neuroendocrine Tumors: Biological Rationale, Combination Strategies, and Clinical Perspectives.
authors: Hana Bakr; Amin Al-Awar; Johan K E Spetz; Eva B Forssell-Aronsson
abstract: ['Gastroenteropancreatic (GEP) neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) are the most common subtype of NETs, and their incidence continues to increase worldwide. Many NETs express somatostatin receptors (SSTRs), enabling molecular imaging and treatment with radiolabeled somatostatin analogs (SSTAs). [<sup>177</sup>Lu]Lu-DOTATATE is an established treatment for advanced SSTR-positive NETs, but complete and durable responses remain uncommon. This review summarizes current clinical experience with [<sup>177</sup>Lu]Lu-DOTATATE and emerging SSTR-targeting radiopharmaceuticals and examines strategies to improve PRRT efficacy. Treatment may be enhanced at several interconnected steps, including increasing receptor availability and tumor targeting, improving radiopharmaceutical uptake and absorbed dose, preventing repair of radiation-induced damage, suppressing cellular stress adaptation and survival, and promoting tumor cell elimination. These approaches include radiation priming and fractionation, somatostatin analog pretreatment, epigenetic modifiers, inhibitors of DNA repair and cellular survival pathways, immunotherapy, and chemotherapy-based combinations. PARP, DNA-PK, and HSP90 inhibitors and chemotherapy-based combinations have shown particularly strong preclinical or clinical evidence, whereas mTOR inhibitors, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, Hedgehog inhibitors, immunotherapy, NAMPT inhibitors, p53 stabilization, and epigenetic modifiers remain under investigation. Ongoing development of novel radiopharmaceuticals, personalized dosimetry, retreatment strategies, and rational combinations is expected to refine PRRT and improve outcomes for patients with NETs.']

title: Toxoplasmosis: Epidemiological Significance, Economic Burden, and Emerging Directions in Drug Discovery and Artificial Intelligence.
authors: Albert Fynn Aiduenu; Blessing Kwabena Gayi; Aboagye Kwarteng Dofuor; Susanna Awinsongya Anovunga; William Ekloh; Joseph Harold Nyarko Osei; Christopher Nii Laryea Tawiah-Mensah; Juliet Ama Mawusi Koudonu Seglah; Jennifer Afua Afrifa Yamoah; Angelina Akomea; Andy Asafu-Adjaye
abstract: ["Toxoplasmosis, a parasitic disease caused by Toxoplasma gondii, affects a wide range of warm-blooded hosts and remains most prevalent in tropical regions, with distribution shaped by climate, cultural practices, and environmental conditions. Clinical severity varies across susceptible populations, generating substantial economic burdens through medical costs and agricultural losses. Given this global health impact, a comprehensive, up-to-date understanding of the disease is essential. However, significant gaps persist. While diagnostic techniques and epidemiological surveillance have advanced considerably, treatment protocols have remained largely unchanged for decades, revealing a disconnect between diagnostic innovation and therapeutic progress. Moreover, existing literature lacks an integrative synthesis connecting these advances to their broader significance, leaving researchers without a unified framework for understanding where the field stands and where it should go next. To address these gaps, this narrative review draws on peer-reviewed literature and institutional reports across major biomedical databases, synthesizing findings descriptively and thematically rather than through statistical meta-analysis. It critically examines toxoplasmosis across several dimensions. It first considers geographical distribution and the cultural, environmental, and economic factors shaping its epidemiology. It then turns to the parasite's biochemical and molecular characteristics, using this foundation to evaluate persistent limitations in treatment and vaccine development, an area where progress has stalled. In response, the review explores emerging alternatives, including plant-based compounds, as avenues beyond conventional pharmacological strategies. Finally, it examines artificial intelligence as an underexplored but promising tool for improving diagnosis and treatment, an area with limited application to toxoplasmosis specifically. By consolidating these threads, this review clarifies not only what is known about toxoplasmosis but also where critical gaps in treatment innovation and integrative understanding continue to hinder effective prevention and control."]

title: Do People Still Matter? Healthcare in the Age of Artificial Intelligence.
authors: Julie Haizlip; Katy Hall; Natalie B May
abstract: ['Artificial intelligence (AI) platforms are becoming increasingly prevalent in healthcare. Unlike previous technologies, AI has the capability to perform tasks previously considered uniquely human including synthesizing historical information and data to establish a clinical diagnosis and constructing a treatment plan. AI promises to improve diagnostic accuracy, accelerate drug discovery and development, and enhance access to healthcare. The overall impact that AI will have on the well-being of individuals who provide and receive care, however, is less obvious. This article examines the potential and pitfalls of AI in medicine through the lens of mattering and its importance to human flourishing. Mattering is a psychological construct that encompasses the human needs to be noticed, feel significant, and contribute. It arises from interpersonal interactions and is based on perceptions of our value within our communities and society. Mattering is inherently relational, is a significant contributor to psychological well-being, and may be at risk in the age of AI. The authors describe the foundations of mattering and its relevance to medicine; the potential impacts of AI on mattering in medicine from the clinician, patient, and trainee perspectives; and propose a framework for integrating AI into healthcare such that mattering is preserved for all stakeholders.']

title: Artificial Intelligence in Chronic Rhinosinusitis: From Molecular Profiling to Personalized Clinical Management-A Systematic Review.
authors: Chi-Sheng Huang; Duen-Lii Hsieh; Jin-Yu Lin; Maysayawan Sreesawat; Te-Huei Yeh; Chih-Feng Lin
abstract: ['Chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) is a heterogeneous inflammatory disease imposing a substantial health and economic burden. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool to address CRS complexity in both clinical and research settings. We conducted a systematic review following PRISMA guidelines, searching PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase for peer-reviewed articles utilizing machine learning, deep learning, and natural language processing, with a focus on molecular-level or immunologic mechanisms in CRS. Thirty-one studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. Our results demonstrate that while AI-driven analysis helps stratify patient endotypes, the identified schemes exhibit substantial heterogeneity in cluster numbers and features, raising concerns about their reproducibility. AI applications also included histopathological image interpretation, drug discovery, biologic therapy selection, and prognostic modeling to evaluate revision surgery risks and olfactory dysfunction. However, using the PROBAST+AI framework, we found that 87.1% of the assessed studies carry a high overall risk of bias, mainly due to the reliance on apparent performance or internal validation and limited independent evaluation of model performance, indicating that many reported performance estimates may be optimistic. Future large-scale, multicenter collaborations integrating AI into clinical workflows will be essential to establish reliable and generalizable AI applications for personalized CRS management.']

title: Deep generative models in biological sequence and structure analysis and design.
authors: Fahimeh Palizban; Mohammadmahdi Sarbishegi; Huiqi Qu; Amir Hossein Saeidian; Mahya Mehrmohamadi; Joseph Glessner; Hakon Hakonarson
abstract: ['Deep generative models have transformed biological sequence modeling from predictive analysis toward increasingly controllable design. Early biological applications of Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) established latent representation learning and sequence synthesis, while recent advances in transformer-based language models, discrete diffusion, flow-matching, and multimodal generative frameworks have substantially expanded the scope of biological design. This review examines generative models for DNA, RNA, and protein sequence design, emphasizing how different model classes represent biological constraints, operate over discrete and continuous spaces, and integrate sequence, structure, and function. We compare VAEs, GANs, autoregressive and masked language models, diffusion models, and flow-based approaches across genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics, with particular attention to controllability, long-range dependency modeling, structural grounding, generalization, and experimental utility. We further examine evaluation strategies, out-of-distribution generalization, and closed-loop design-build-test-learn workflows that connect in silico generation with empirical validation. We distinguish fundamental modality-dependent constraints including sequence discreteness, context length, structural coupling, and physical or thermodynamic requirements from architecture-dependent advantages that reflect the current state of the field. Current studies suggest that long-context models are particularly useful for genome-scale representation and sequence modeling, whereas structure-aware diffusion, flow-based, and inverse-folding approaches provide better frameworks for geometry-constrained RNA and protein design. This perspective provides a critical framework for understanding the present capabilities, limitations, and convergence of generative approaches toward reliable and experimentally grounded biological design.']

title: Rett syndrome: MECP2 biology, multisystem pathophysiology, and the evolving therapeutic landscape.
authors: S T Gopukumar; Madhumita Saha; Sahil Bhardwaj; Kesavaperumal Gopalakrishnan; Eid Semer Alatwi; Rasha Alonaizan; Huda A Alqahtani; Tanveen Kaur Soni; Samer Shamshad; Uddalak Das
abstract: [StringElement('Rett syndrome (RTT) is an X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder arising predominantly from de novo loss-of-function mutations in MECP2, affecting approximately 1 in 10,000 live female births. MECP2 is a dosage-sensitive epigenetic regulator acting through its methyl-CpG-binding (MBD) and transcriptional-repression (TRD) domains; isoform-specific expression and X-chromosome-inactivation mosaicism drive the wide phenotypic variability, with mutation type broadly correlating with severity. Although historically viewed as neuron-centric, RTT is a multisystem disorder: beyond psychomotor regression, stereotypic hand movements, gait apraxia, and loss of spoken language, MECP2 deficiency contributes to brainstem-mediated breathing dysrhythmia, QTc prolongation, enteric dysmotility, low bone density, and mitochondrial/metabolic deficits, amplified by glial-neuronal crosstalk. Preclinical models, MECP2 rodents, patient iPSC-derived neurons, and cerebral organoids, reveal synaptic and dendritic deficits that improve substantially when MECP2 is reactivated in these systems, indicating that MECP2-deficient neurons remain viable rather than degenerating; whether comparable improvement can be achieved in affected individuals is not yet established. The therapeutic landscape now spans multidisciplinary supportive care, the first approved pharmacotherapy trofinetide, AAV-mediated MECP2 gene replacement (now in pivotal trials, with an important gene-therapy safety signal), antisense oligonucleotides for dosage normalisation, and emerging metabolic agents; validated biomarkers and objective outcome measures remain a major unmet need.', attributes={'Label': 'UNLABELLED'}), StringElement('RTT is a multisystem monogenic disorder whose management is shifting from symptom control toward disease modification. Phenotypic rescue after MECP2 restoration in rodent models provides the rationale for this shift but does not establish that RTT is reversible in patients; progress now depends on validated biomarkers, dose-controlled disease-modifying therapies, long-term outcome data, and equitable global access.', attributes={'Label': 'CONCLUSION', 'NlmCategory': 'CONCLUSIONS'}), StringElement('• More than 90-95% of classic Rett syndrome is caused by de novo loss-of-function mutations in MECP2, a dosage-sensitive epigenetic reader whose isoform distribution, residual function and X-chromosome-inactivation mosaicism together account for much of the phenotypic variability. • Reactivating MECP2 in symptomatic adult rodents substantially improves many disease features, establishing that MECP2-deficient neurons are functionally impaired rather than lost and providing the rationale for disease-modifying therapy.', attributes={'Label': 'WHAT IS KNOWN', 'NlmCategory': 'BACKGROUND'}), StringElement('•\xa0This review integrates isoform-specific and non-neuronal (glial, respiratory, cardiac, gastrointestinal, skeletal and metabolic) mechanisms with a literature base updated to 15 August 2026, and identifies the continuing absence of any validated biomarker or surrogate endpoint, rather than target identification, as the principal obstacle to efficient trials. •\xa0It critically appraises the post-trofinetide landscape - divergent FDA and EMA assessments of the same trial data, a fatal high-dose AAV hyperinflammatory event, and single-arm registrational gene-therapy programmes reported largely outside peer review - and concludes that the demonstrated outcome to date is gain or re-acquisition of developmental milestones, not reversal of established disease.', attributes={'Label': 'WHAT IS NEW', 'NlmCategory': 'BACKGROUND'})]

title: Multi-objective antibody design and optimization using machine learning.
authors: Yun-Huai Kuo; Chloe N Brown; Ece Akin; Yunxuan Xie; Peter M Tessier
abstract: ['Antibodies, ranging from conventional immunoglobulins to single-domain and bispecific antibodies, are developed for a wide spectrum of therapeutic and diagnostic applications. However, lead antibodies are commonly engineered to optimize one or more key properties, including affinity, specificity, polyreactivity, stability, aggregation, and immunogenicity, and tradeoffs among these attributes frequently hinder the development of variants suitable for clinical use. Furthermore, identifying lead candidates with desirable properties typically requires multiple rounds of experimental screening and evaluation, particularly when targeting pre-selected epitopes or challenging, high-value targets such as G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), ion channels, and multipass membrane proteins. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods can streamline experimental screening and antibody generation methods. In this Review, we discuss both computational multi-objective optimization of existing antibodies and de novo antibody design. The application of AI/ML methods has the potential to overcome current bottlenecks in antibody development and accelerate the generation of improved therapeutics for human health.']

title: Peptide surface structure flexibility controls gold nanoparticle uptake in triple-negative breast cancer cells.
authors: Suranjana Chakrabarty; Manash Sarkar; Sudipta Saha; Souhadri Das; Koyel Howlader; Nirmalya Sen; Anjan Barman; Anup Ghosh
abstract: ['Peptide-functionalized gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) provide a model for decoding how the surface-bound secondary structure regulates nano-bio interactions. AuNPs (30-40 nm) coated with small peptides, GSH, ECECG, GSSG and cyclic CEIEIEC exhibited a progressive increment in antiparallel β-sheet content (37-89%) upon surface binding with an increase in the number of amino acids. Cellular studies in MDA-MB-231 cells revealed efficient uptake for flexible, mixed-structure coronas (GSH, ECECG, GSSG), while the rigid, antiparallel β-sheet-dominant cyclic CEIEIEC corona suppressed internalization despite full cytocompatibility. These findings suggest that peptide conformational adaptability is associated with cellular entry, suggesting a clear structure-uptake relationship for the design of peptide-AuNP nanocarriers in aggressive breast cancer.']

title: Peptides in urology and sexual medicine: clinical effectiveness, dosing, indications, and safety: a narrative review.
authors: Valeriia Vasylieva; Annette West; Edward Karpman
abstract: [StringElement('Peptide-based therapies are increasingly used in urology and sexual medicine, although adoption is often influenced by off-label prescribing, direct-to-consumer promotion, and limited long-term safety data. We review mechanisms, clinical evidence, dosing, safety, and regulatory status of these agents.', attributes={'Label': 'INTRODUCTION', 'NlmCategory': 'BACKGROUND'}), StringElement('A structured search of PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar identified studies of peptide-based therapies in sexual medicine. Search terms included Bremelanotide, Melanotan II, Kisspeptin, Oxytocin, PnPP-19, Gonadorelin and growth hormone secretagogues, including GHRP-2, GHRP-6, Ibutamoren, Ipamorelin, Tesamorelin, Sermorelin, and CJC-1295. Of 725 records, 76 studies met inclusion criteria. Findings were synthesized narratively given heterogeneity across studies.', attributes={'Label': 'METHODS', 'NlmCategory': 'METHODS'}), StringElement('Peptides reviewed act through diverse mechanisms, including central modulation of desire and arousal, stimulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal and growth hormone axes, and nitric oxide-mediated effects on erectile physiology. Bremelanotide and Tesamorelin are the most clinically established agents, with defined dosing and regulatory approval for selected indications. Kisspeptin shows early promise but remains investigational. Growth hormone secretagogues reliably increase growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor 1 concentrations; however, evidence for improved sexual function, physical performance, or quality of life remains limited. Melanotan II, Ibutamoren, CJC-1295, and related agents remain accessible through unregulated markets, raising concerns about product quality, dosing variability, and incompletely characterized adverse effects. Oxytocin has biologic plausibility but limited efficacy data, whereas PnPP-19 remains preclinical. Gonadorelin was Food and Drug Administration approved but is no longer manufactured. Across peptide classes, safety data are limited by short follow-up, small samples, and incomplete assessment of cardiovascular, metabolic, and oncologic outcomes.', attributes={'Label': 'RESULTS', 'NlmCategory': 'RESULTS'}), StringElement('Peptide-based therapies in urology and sexual medicine show selective therapeutic potential, but most remain insufficiently validated for clinical use. Clinicians should distinguish approved therapies from investigational and nonregulated compounds and counsel patients regarding uncertain benefit, potential harm, and risks of unsupervised use. Randomized trials with standardized dosing and long-term safety assessment are needed before broader adoption.', attributes={'Label': 'DISCUSSION', 'NlmCategory': 'CONCLUSIONS'})]

title: Advances in Somatostatin Receptor-Targeting Peptide Receptor Radionuclide Therapy for Neuroendocrine Tumors: Biological Rationale, Combination Strategies, and Clinical Perspectives.
authors: Hana Bakr; Amin Al-Awar; Johan K E Spetz; Eva B Forssell-Aronsson
abstract: ['Gastroenteropancreatic (GEP) neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) are the most common subtype of NETs, and their incidence continues to increase worldwide. Many NETs express somatostatin receptors (SSTRs), enabling molecular imaging and treatment with radiolabeled somatostatin analogs (SSTAs). [<sup>177</sup>Lu]Lu-DOTATATE is an established treatment for advanced SSTR-positive NETs, but complete and durable responses remain uncommon. This review summarizes current clinical experience with [<sup>177</sup>Lu]Lu-DOTATATE and emerging SSTR-targeting radiopharmaceuticals and examines strategies to improve PRRT efficacy. Treatment may be enhanced at several interconnected steps, including increasing receptor availability and tumor targeting, improving radiopharmaceutical uptake and absorbed dose, preventing repair of radiation-induced damage, suppressing cellular stress adaptation and survival, and promoting tumor cell elimination. These approaches include radiation priming and fractionation, somatostatin analog pretreatment, epigenetic modifiers, inhibitors of DNA repair and cellular survival pathways, immunotherapy, and chemotherapy-based combinations. PARP, DNA-PK, and HSP90 inhibitors and chemotherapy-based combinations have shown particularly strong preclinical or clinical evidence, whereas mTOR inhibitors, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, Hedgehog inhibitors, immunotherapy, NAMPT inhibitors, p53 stabilization, and epigenetic modifiers remain under investigation. Ongoing development of novel radiopharmaceuticals, personalized dosimetry, retreatment strategies, and rational combinations is expected to refine PRRT and improve outcomes for patients with NETs.']

title: Exploring Potential Multi-Target Inhibition Mechanisms of Ganoderma lucidum Against EBV-Mediated DLBCL Using Integrative Bioinformatics, Machine Learning, and Network Pharmacology Approaches.
authors: Azrin Ahmed; Md Abdul Kader; Sheikh Abdullah Al Ashik
abstract: ['Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-associated diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) represents a significant clinical challenge with limited targeted therapeutic options. Despite the known antiviral and anticancer properties of Ganoderma lucidum, its specific molecular mechanisms against EBV-mediated DLBCL remain unexplored. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the potential multi-target inhibitory mechanisms of G. lucidum compounds against EBV-associated DLBCL by integrating absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) profiling of 1046 compounds; network pharmacology analysis for target identification; transcriptomic evaluation using DLBCL patient datasets from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) (n\xa0=\xa047 tumors, n\xa0=\xa0337 normals); molecular docking; density functional theory (DFT) calculations; machine learning-based activity prediction, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations; and Molecular Mechanics Poisson-Boltzmann Surface Area (MM-PBSA) binding free energy calculations. Eight compounds (kobusin, chrysin, dalbergin, galangin, isorhamnetin, lauric acid, piperbetol, and vitamin D3) demonstrated favorable ADMET profiles. Network pharmacology analysis identified 217 common targets, with AKT1 and BCL2 significantly upregulated in DLBCL tumors. Isorhamnetin showed the strongest AKT1 binding (-8.33\xa0kcal/mol), surpassing control (-5.11\xa0kcal/mol), whereas galangin exhibited the highest BCL2 affinity (-6.13\xa0kcal/mol), outperforming control (-5.23\xa0kcal/mol). Random forest achieved cross-validation scores of 0.8634\xa0±\xa00.0158 for AKT1 and 0.8965\xa0±\xa00.0146 for BCL2, predicting IC<sub>50</sub> <1000\xa0nM for all compounds. MD simulations confirmed the binding stability of all compounds with low root mean square deviation (RMSD, <2.5\xa0Å). MM-PBSA calculations revealed favorable binding free energies of -23.01\xa0kcal/mol (AKT1-galangin), -19.01\xa0kcal/mol (AKT1-isorhamnetin), -32.15\xa0kcal/mol (BCL2-isorhamnetin), and -28.97\xa0kcal/mol (BCL2-galangin). Therefore, isorhamnetin and galangin may have multi-target inhibitory potential against AKT1 and BCL2, providing a robust foundation for further in vitro and in vivo validation as therapeutic candidates for EBV-mediated DLBCL intervention. PRACTICAL APPLICATIONS: Ganoderma lucidum is a medicinal mushroom widely used in traditional and functional food applications and may serve as a source of natural anticancer compounds with potential benefits for EBV-associated diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. The multi-targeting potential of G. lucidum-derived bioactive constituents, isorhamnetin and galangin, against AKT1 and BCL2 may position it as a promising functional food-based candidate for anticancer therapeutics.']

title: qcGEM: A Graph-Based Molecular Representation With Quantum Chemistry Awareness.
authors: Haoyu Wang; Ziyan Zhang; Swee Hong Ng; Haipeng Gong
abstract: ['The advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has reshaped drug discovery. AI-based models typically rely on molecular representations for prediction. However, the absence of physically grounded information in mainstream molecular representations not only limits the model performance in practical applications but also hinders mechanistic understanding and exploitation by humans. To overcome this issue, we introduce qcGEM, a quantum-chemistry-aware graph-based embedding of molecules that incorporates physical priors into molecular representation learning. Through a specially designed model architecture to adequately process quantum chemistry information, qcGEM provides a compact, physics-informed molecular representation that supports a diverse range of downstream applications. Particularly, qcGEM demonstrates state-of-the-art performance across a broad range of molecule-related benchmarks, as evidenced by comprehensive evaluations on 83 tasks including molecular property prediction, activity cliff detection, protein-ligand interaction modeling, and opioid drug regression, and simultaneously offers strong interpretability at multiple representation levels. We additionally propose a simplified variant, qcGEM-Hybrid, with substantially accelerated embedding generation and robust performance. Overall, our method provides an advanced molecular representation that will benefit molecule-related modeling and prediction, supporting further progress in AI-aided drug\xa0discovery.']

title: Sampling protein language models for functional protein design.
authors: Jeremie Theddy Darmawan; Yarin Gal; Pascal Notin
abstract: ['Protein language models have emerged as powerful tools for learning rich protein representations, improving tasks like structure prediction, mutation effect estimation, and homology detection. Their ability to model complex sequence distributions also holds promise for designing novel, functional proteins with applications in therapeutics, materials, and sustainability. Given the vastness of sequence space, efficient exploration is essential. However, most existing design approaches rely on single-mutant sampling strategies borrowed from natural language processing, which fail to capture epistatic interactions critical for function. Here, we develop an in silico framework to systematically compare sampling methods and introduce several approaches tailored for protein design. We show that sampling multiple mutations simultaneously substantially outperforms single-mutant approaches by better capturing epistatic effects. We evaluate these strategies across three protein families spanning eukaryotic, prokaryotic, and viral origins, examine key hyperparameters, and validate our findings on a de novo binder design task against a major therapeutic target.']

title: Multi-parameter optimization of recombinant protein secretion in Bacillus subtilis: a review.
authors: Askar Kholikov; Khushnut Vokhidov; Barno Alimova; Ozodakhon Pulatova; Yulong Zhang; Shihui Yang; Guimin Zhang; Yihua Chen; Akhmadzhan Makhsumkhanov
abstract: ['Bacillus subtilis is widely recognized as one of the most robust and versatile hosts for recombinant protein production. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the protein secretion pathway in B. subtilis, detailing its mechanistic basis and key limiting steps. We discuss the structural features of signal peptides (SPs) that govern efficient translocation and highlight recent advances in de novo promoter and signal peptide engineering. A particular focus is placed on the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) to predict and design optimal genetic elements. Drawing on findings from combinatorial and multi-parameter studies, we propose that future engineering strategies should move beyond maximizing individual parameters. Instead, achieving a dynamic balance across transcriptional, translational and secretion layers is essential to sustain high productivity while minimizing cellular secretion stress. This review offers a roadmap for systems-level engineering of B. subtilis as a next-generation protein production platform.']

title: Small-molecule activators of the Staphylococcus aureus ClpC/ClpP AAA+ protease.
authors: Timo Jenne; Vsevolod Viliuga; Ulrike Uhrig; Britta Jehle; Merlin Schwan; Jürgen Kopp; Dirk Flemming; Elisabeth Seebach; Irmgard Sinning; Bernd Bukau; Axel Mogk
abstract: ['The central AAA+ ClpC/ClpP protease in Gram-positive bacteria is crucial for virulence and stress resistance and has been recognized as drug target. Natural cyclic peptides deregulate the essential Mycobacterium tuberculosis ClpC1 and cause cell death. Similarly, overactivated mutants of the non-essential Staphylococcus aureus ClpC homolog cause uncontrolled proteolysis and severe toxicity in vivo. However, no chemical modulators of S. aureus ClpC have been described. Here, using a biochemical high-throughput screen, we identify eight distinct bona fide small molecules that stimulate ClpC ATPase and proteolytic activity in vitro. Structural, computational, and mutational analyses define two ligandable regulatory sites within the ClpC N-terminal domain (NTD) as compound targets: a conserved hydrophobic groove and an allosteric pArg1 pocket, both engaged in substrate recognition. These findings establish S. aureus ClpC as chemically targetable and provide mechanistic insight into its regulatory architecture, enabling future development and optimization of chemical probes to deregulate AAA+ protease control.']

title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Parasitology: A holistic perspective from diagnosis to therapeutics.
authors: Muhammet Uslug; Figen Celik; Sami Simsek
abstract: ['Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being investigated to address challenges in parasite detection, disease surveillance, and therapeutic development. This narrative review examines current and emerging AI applications in parasitology across diagnostics, drug discovery, genomics, epidemiology, education, and public health decision-making, with particular emphasis on diagnostic applications. Machine learning and deep learning methods support automated parasite detection, classification, and quantification in microscopic images, alongside medical image analysis and arthropod identification. Applications are discussed for malaria, leishmaniasis, schistosomiasis, cystic echinococcosis, soil-transmitted helminth infections, and intestinal protozoal infections. Beyond diagnosis, AI-assisted approaches support compound screening, drug repurposing, toxicity prediction, and prioritization of potential therapeutic targets. Genomic and transcriptomic analyses also offer opportunities to investigate parasite biology and predict drug resistance. Surveillance models may inform outbreak forecasting and targeted control, although their operational value requires evaluation in the intended settings. Educational applications remain emerging, and the benefits of digital learning should be distinguished from those attributable specifically to AI. Across these domains, performance on curated datasets does not establish clinical utility or generalizability. Major barriers include limited representative datasets, insufficient external and prospective validation, infrastructure constraints, and concerns regarding privacy, bias, and accountability. Future progress requires reproducible evaluation, experimental validation of therapeutic candidates, and assessment of clinical and public health benefits. AI is therefore best positioned as a complementary tool that supports parasitological expertise, with responsible implementation guided by transparency, equitable access, and human oversight.']

title: A new era of GPCR drug discovery: From receptor deorphanization to precision therapeutics.
authors: Hidetoshi Komatsu
journal: Proceedings of the Japan Academy. Series B, Physical and biological sciences
abstract: ['G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) play central roles in the regulation of physiology and disease and constitute the largest family of therapeutic targets. Over the past several decades, GPCR-targeted medicines have transformed the treatment of numerous disorders. A major turning point in the field was the deorphanization of previously uncharacterized receptors, which not only expanded the repertoire of therapeutic targets but also revealed unexpected physiological functions and disease mechanisms. At the same time, advances in molecular and cellular pharmacology have demonstrated that GPCR signaling is far more complex than originally envisioned. Receptor responses are shaped by cellular context, signaling networks, transcriptional regulation, and temporal and spatial dynamics, resulting in diverse physiological and pathological outcomes. More recently, innovations in structural biology, computational science, artificial intelligence, and systems biology have accelerated target identification and therapeutic design. Together, these advances are transforming GPCR drug discovery from traditional screening approaches toward a systems-level understanding of disease biology and precision therapeutic intervention. This review summarizes the historical evolution of GPCR drug discovery, highlights major conceptual breakthroughs that have reshaped the field, and discusses future opportunities and challenges that may define a new era of GPCR drug discovery.']

title: IHLO-DTI: Drug-Target Interaction Prediction Based on Improved Hypergraph Neural Network and Laplacian Matrix Optimization.
authors: Guolongwei Dai; Tao Luo; Dandan Li; Zeping Liu; Jiaying Gu; Lingjie Fan; Tao Lin; Quan Wei; Fengyi Wang
abstract: ['Accurate prediction of drug-target interactions is pivotal for accelerating drug discovery and drug repurposing. However, existing advanced methods often fail to effectively characterize the many-to-many interactions between drugs and targets. Furthermore, they struggle to fully mine the structural features of drugs and proteins. To address these limitations, we propose IHLO-DTI, a novel prediction model based on an improved hypergraph neural network and Laplacian matrix optimization. First, we construct drug, protein, and drug-protein pair hypergraphs, where shared-drug and shared-target relationships are used to characterize multi-target activity and shared-target regulation. We then optimize hyperedge weights using a Laplacian matrix to enhance biologically meaningful high-order associations and suppress potential noise. Second, we use simplified graph convolution and graph convolutional network to extract global and local features, enabling efficient modeling of multi-level semantic information for drugs and targets. Next, we introduce a cross-attention mechanism and a dynamic gating module to perform fine-grained fusion of multi-channel features, improving the representation of cross-modal information interactions. Finally, we jointly train the model with contrastive learning and cross-entropy loss to enhance the consistency and discriminability of the learned representations. IHLO-DTI achieves mean AUROC and AUPR values of 0.9777 and 0.9716, respectively, on two public datasets. IHLO-DTI can effectively capture high-order many-to-many interactions between drugs and targets, improving prediction accuracy and robustness. It provides a more reliable computational tool for clinical drug screening, repurposing, and precision medicine research.']

title: Multi-objective antibody design and optimization using machine learning.
authors: Yun-Huai Kuo; Chloe N Brown; Ece Akin; Yunxuan Xie; Peter M Tessier
abstract: ['Antibodies, ranging from conventional immunoglobulins to single-domain and bispecific antibodies, are developed for a wide spectrum of therapeutic and diagnostic applications. However, lead antibodies are commonly engineered to optimize one or more key properties, including affinity, specificity, polyreactivity, stability, aggregation, and immunogenicity, and tradeoffs among these attributes frequently hinder the development of variants suitable for clinical use. Furthermore, identifying lead candidates with desirable properties typically requires multiple rounds of experimental screening and evaluation, particularly when targeting pre-selected epitopes or challenging, high-value targets such as G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), ion channels, and multipass membrane proteins. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods can streamline experimental screening and antibody generation methods. In this Review, we discuss both computational multi-objective optimization of existing antibodies and de novo antibody design. The application of AI/ML methods has the potential to overcome current bottlenecks in antibody development and accelerate the generation of improved therapeutics for human health.']

title: Multi-parameter optimization of recombinant protein secretion in Bacillus subtilis: a review.
authors: Askar Kholikov; Khushnut Vokhidov; Barno Alimova; Ozodakhon Pulatova; Yulong Zhang; Shihui Yang; Guimin Zhang; Yihua Chen; Akhmadzhan Makhsumkhanov
abstract: ['Bacillus subtilis is widely recognized as one of the most robust and versatile hosts for recombinant protein production. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the protein secretion pathway in B. subtilis, detailing its mechanistic basis and key limiting steps. We discuss the structural features of signal peptides (SPs) that govern efficient translocation and highlight recent advances in de novo promoter and signal peptide engineering. A particular focus is placed on the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) to predict and design optimal genetic elements. Drawing on findings from combinatorial and multi-parameter studies, we propose that future engineering strategies should move beyond maximizing individual parameters. Instead, achieving a dynamic balance across transcriptional, translational and secretion layers is essential to sustain high productivity while minimizing cellular secretion stress. This review offers a roadmap for systems-level engineering of B. subtilis as a next-generation protein production platform.']

title: Generating protein hydrogels with customizable stress relaxation behavior via deep learning-driven entanglement design.
authors: Puqing Deng; Yutong Wu; Hong Kiu Francis Fok; Linyan Li; Wen-Bin Zhang; Fei Sun; Hanyu Gao
abstract: ['Protein hydrogels are promising artificial extracellular matrices (ECMs) for 3D stem cell and organoid culture due to their favorable stress relaxation behavior (a decrease in stress in response to strain). Inter-chain entangled motifs, in which different protein chains are interlaced, represent a powerful strategy to synthesize such hydrogels. However, designing these motifs with tailored properties such as binding energy remains a major challenge due to the difficulty of simultaneously controlling these properties while ensuring entanglement. Here, we introduce TangleDiff, a deep learning framework for the de novo design of homodimeric entangled proteins with programmable features. TangleDiff generates diverse foldable entangled sequences with an in-silico success rate exceeding 70%, markedly outperforming current models (~1%). By conditioning TangleDiff on inter-chain binding energy, we generate novel protein dimers whose binding energies closely match the specified ranges, with approximately 70% of successful designs conforming to expected values. We experimentally validate TangleDiff by designing nine homodimers targeting various binding energies; seven successfully form hydrogels, with stress relaxation dynamics correlated with specified binding energies. This work establishes a general strategy for entangled protein design, opening avenues for entanglement-based biomaterial innovation.']

title: Bacterial Display of Genetically Encoded Macrocyclic Peptide Libraries Using Cysteine-Reactive Unnatural Amino Acids.
authors: Olabode Dawodu; Jeffery M Tharp
abstract: ['Cyclic peptides are powerful scaffolds for modulating protein-protein interactions; however, methods for constructing cyclic peptide libraries for cell-surface display applications remain limited. Here, we present a bacterial surface display platform that enables site-specific incorporation of diverse unnatural amino acids (uAAs) into peptides displayed on the surface of Escherichia coli. These uAAs include several cysteine-reactive residues that undergo spontaneous intramolecular reactions with cysteine to generate macrocyclic peptides directly on the bacterial outer membrane. Using high-resolution mass spectrometry, we show that peptide cyclization proceeds efficiently and selectively with no detectable off-target reactions. Further, we demonstrate that this platform supports simultaneous incorporation of two distinct uAAs, enabling the surface display of chemically diverse, drug-like macrocycles. To demonstrate the utility of this platform, we constructed and screened a naïve macrocyclic peptide library against a model target, yielding de novo ligands with conserved sequence motifs and binding affinities similar to those previously identified by phage display. Together, these results establish a robust approach for generating diverse cyclic peptide libraries, thereby expanding the scope of cell-surface display for research and drug discovery.']

title: DynlogPA Novel High-Throughput LC-MS Assay Quantifying Dynamic Lipophilicity and Chameleonicity of bRo5 Macrocyclic Peptides.
authors: Christian Weinmann; Franz Waibl; Silvan Käser; Fabio Casagrande; Jitao David Zhang; Fabian Dey; Björn Wagner; Britta Schulze; Carsten Kroll; Janneke Keemink
abstract: ['The landscape of drug discovery has expanded beyond the traditional chemical space into the domain of large, flexible molecules, including beyond rule-of-five (bRo5) macrocyclic peptides (MCPs). Molecular chameleonicity, the capacity to dynamically adapt the conformation to the environment, balancing aqueous solubility and membrane permeability, has the potential to improve the oral bioavailability of these compounds. However, we lack experimental methods that quantify chameleonicity in a high-throughput manner. To address this need, we introduce DynlogP, a novel high-throughput, fully automated assay based on reverse-phase LC-MS that can quantify chameleonicity with minimal compound input. DynlogP measures calibrated lipophilicity under conditions promoting either solvent hydrogen bonding (log P70) or intramolecular hydrogen bonding (log P95), providing a quantitative measure of chameleonicity (Δlog P95-70) that is validated with NMR and molecular dynamics simulations. We profiled hundreds of molecules with DynlogP and demonstrate that chameleonicity is a common feature of MCPs. Machine learning models trained with DynlogP data allow for the prospective prediction of chameleonicity. Adoption and further refinement of DynlogP have the potential to empower compound prioritization and the design of orally bioavailable MCP-based therapeutics.']

title: Dual Roles of Cyanopeptides as Substrates and Inhibitors of Enzymes in Surface Waters.
authors: Xuejian Wang; Elena Lippuner; Yaochun Yu; Elisabeth M L Janssen
abstract: ["Harmful cyanobacterial blooms produce diverse bioactive metabolites, cyanopeptides, whose environmental persistence remains uncertain. First, we investigated enzymatic reactions with cyanopeptides as substrates in aquatic systems. The aquatic enzyme pool from the riverine biofilm showed peptidase and oxidase activities. Incubation of cyanopeptides with the natural aquatic enzyme pool revealed novel transformation products (TPs) of two microginins (nostoginin BN741 and microginin FR6) and TPs of anabaenopeptins that also formed when incubated with intact biofilm. Next, we probed underlying mechanisms with peptidases as functional analogs of the aquatic enzyme pool. Carboxypeptidase Y produced identical hydrolysis TPs of the two microginins. A multicopper oxidase rapidly transformed tyrosine-containing microcystins, anabaenopeptins, and microginins, in the presence of the mediator 2,2'-azinobis(3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonate) (ABTS). Tyrosine-free congeners remained stable. Lastly, we investigated cyanopeptides as enzyme inhibitors. Cyanopeptolins inhibited trypsin (IC50 = 53.75 nM), chymotrypsin (IC50 = 2.2 μM), and analogous activities in the aquatic enzyme pool. Anabaenopeptins and microginins showed only mild inhibition of carboxypeptidase Y. As different cyanopeptides are co-produced by cyanobacteria, biotransformation is expected to differ in mixtures compared to single-compound assessments due to the observed inhibition taking place at the same time. Similarly, their release during bloom events may influence the transformation of other organic compounds in surface waters."]

title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Parasitology: A holistic perspective from diagnosis to therapeutics.
authors: Muhammet Uslug; Figen Celik; Sami Simsek
abstract: ['Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being investigated to address challenges in parasite detection, disease surveillance, and therapeutic development. This narrative review examines current and emerging AI applications in parasitology across diagnostics, drug discovery, genomics, epidemiology, education, and public health decision-making, with particular emphasis on diagnostic applications. Machine learning and deep learning methods support automated parasite detection, classification, and quantification in microscopic images, alongside medical image analysis and arthropod identification. Applications are discussed for malaria, leishmaniasis, schistosomiasis, cystic echinococcosis, soil-transmitted helminth infections, and intestinal protozoal infections. Beyond diagnosis, AI-assisted approaches support compound screening, drug repurposing, toxicity prediction, and prioritization of potential therapeutic targets. Genomic and transcriptomic analyses also offer opportunities to investigate parasite biology and predict drug resistance. Surveillance models may inform outbreak forecasting and targeted control, although their operational value requires evaluation in the intended settings. Educational applications remain emerging, and the benefits of digital learning should be distinguished from those attributable specifically to AI. Across these domains, performance on curated datasets does not establish clinical utility or generalizability. Major barriers include limited representative datasets, insufficient external and prospective validation, infrastructure constraints, and concerns regarding privacy, bias, and accountability. Future progress requires reproducible evaluation, experimental validation of therapeutic candidates, and assessment of clinical and public health benefits. AI is therefore best positioned as a complementary tool that supports parasitological expertise, with responsible implementation guided by transparency, equitable access, and human oversight.']

title: Construction of Matrix Metalloproteinase-13-Activatable cRGD-Targeted Ratiometric Fluorescent Nanoprobe for Imaging Microscopic Osteosarcoma Lesions and Pulmonary Metastases.
authors: Yunkai Bao; Shasha Li; Yanqi Wang; Zhenxin Wang; Xiurong Yang
abstract: ['As an important matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) family member, MMP-13 is involved in collagen degradation, extracellular matrix remodeling, and tumor invasion and metastasis, which represents a promising molecular target for activity-based detection of osteosarcoma (OS)-associated lesions. Based on this feature, an MMP-13-activatable, cyclic Arg-Gly-Asp (cRGD)-targeted ratiometric fluorescent nanoprobe, UCNP@PDA@Cy5-pep-cRGD, has been constructed through immobilization of Cy5 modified MMP-13 peptide substrate with cRGD motif (Cy5-pep-cRGD) on the polydopamine coated upconversion nanoparticle (UCNP@PDA). In this nanoprobe, UCNP is employed as a stable upconversion luminescence (UCL) reference, polydopamine (PDA) is used as a low-background fluorescence-quenching platform, Cy5 is modified on an MMP-13-cleavable peptide substrate as the responsive signal, and cRGD is further modified on the nanoprobe surface to enhance its tumor-targeted accumulation. The nanoprobe has been systematically characterized, and evaluated for MMP-13 responsiveness, selectivity, ratiometric detection performance, and biological stability. Cellular experiments demonstrate that UCNP@PDA@Cy5-pep-cRGD has strong targeted accumulation and enzyme-responsive imaging capability toward tumor cells. In vivo and ex vivo imaging experiments further confirm its ability to visualize MMP-13-responsive activation in microscopic OS lesions and pulmonary metastases. This strategy enables in situ visualization of MMP-13-mediated nanoprobe activation for the identification of microscopic OS lesions and pulmonary metastases.']

title: Exploiting Bridged Conformations for Precise Molecular Recognition in the Design of KRAS-Selective, Orally Available Macrocyclic Peptides.
authors: Mirai Kage; Hatsuo Kawada; Koji Takano; Atsushi Matsuo; Yoshihisa Murata; Satoshi Hashimoto; Minoru Tamiya; Tomoya Kotake; Shino Kuramoto; Takashi Yamano; Machiko Irie; Kazuhiro Ohara; Yuuji Sakurai; Kenichi Nomura; Yuya Morita; Ryuji Hayashi; Yuma Wakamiya; Kana Takei; Hiroshi Tanaka; Yoshikazu Nishimura; Hitoshi Iikura; Takuya Shiraishi; Mikimasa Tanada
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: ['Macrocyclic peptides are attracting attention as a promising therapeutic modality for addressing intracellular targets that are traditionally difficult to address with conventional small molecules or antibodies. In this study, we present the chemical optimization process behind the development of AUBE00 (AP7400, compound 30), a KRAS-selective inhibitor based on a scaffold similar to LUNA18, an orally bioavailable macrocyclic peptide RAS inhibitor. Achieving KRAS isoform selectivity is exceptionally challenging due to the nearly identical backbone structures of KRAS, HRAS, and NRAS (Cα RMSD < 1.1 Å). The success of this study relied on two critical factors: (1) achieving conformational control of the flexible N-alkyl group through a bridging structure linked to the adjacent side chain, which enabled the exploitation of subtle interaction energy differences among the isoforms; and (2) overcoming the trade-off between improved KRAS selectivity and reduced permeability associated with P-glycoprotein (P-gp) substrate liability by employing a modified Caco-2 membrane permeability assay to recover oral bioavailability. Our results demonstrate that a conformational rigidification through a bridged scaffold, implemented while preserving membrane permeability, is a highly effective strategy for achieving isoform selectivity. This study establishes a generalizable design principle for orally bioavailable macrocyclic peptides targeting intracellular proteins that require mutation or isoform selectivity.']

Incubation of cyanopeptides with the natural aquatic enzyme pool revealed novel transformation products (TPs) of two microginins (nostoginin BN741 and microginin FR6) and TPs of anabaenopeptins that also formed when incubated with intact biofilm. Next, we probed underlying mechanisms with peptidases as functional analogs of the aquatic enzyme pool. Carboxypeptidase Y produced identical hydrolysis TPs of the two microginins. A multicopper oxidase rapidly transformed tyrosine-containing microcystins, anabaenopeptins, and microginins, in the presence of the mediator 2,2'-azinobis(3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonate) (ABTS). Tyrosine-free congeners remained stable. Lastly, we investigated cyanopeptides as enzyme inhibitors. Cyanopeptolins inhibited trypsin (IC50 = 53.75 nM), chymotrypsin (IC50 = 2.2 μM), and analogous activities in the aquatic enzyme pool. Anabaenopeptins and microginins showed only mild inhibition of carboxypeptidase Y. As different cyanopeptides are co-produced by cyanobacteria, biotransformation is expected to differ in mixtures compared to single-compound assessments due to the observed inhibition taking place at the same time. Similarly, their release during bloom events may influence the transformation of other organic compounds in surface waters."]

title: Construction of Matrix Metalloproteinase-13-Activatable cRGD-Targeted Ratiometric Fluorescent Nanoprobe for Imaging Microscopic Osteosarcoma Lesions and Pulmonary Metastases.
authors: Yunkai Bao; Shasha Li; Yanqi Wang; Zhenxin Wang; Xiurong Yang
abstract: ['As an important matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) family member, MMP-13 is involved in collagen degradation, extracellular matrix remodeling, and tumor invasion and metastasis, which represents a promising molecular target for activity-based detection of osteosarcoma (OS)-associated lesions. Based on this feature, an MMP-13-activatable, cyclic Arg-Gly-Asp (cRGD)-targeted ratiometric fluorescent nanoprobe, UCNP@PDA@Cy5-pep-cRGD, has been constructed through immobilization of Cy5 modified MMP-13 peptide substrate with cRGD motif (Cy5-pep-cRGD) on the polydopamine coated upconversion nanoparticle (UCNP@PDA). In this nanoprobe, UCNP is employed as a stable upconversion luminescence (UCL) reference, polydopamine (PDA) is used as a low-background fluorescence-quenching platform, Cy5 is modified on an MMP-13-cleavable peptide substrate as the responsive signal, and cRGD is further modified on the nanoprobe surface to enhance its tumor-targeted accumulation. The nanoprobe has been systematically characterized, and evaluated for MMP-13 responsiveness, selectivity, ratiometric detection performance, and biological stability. Cellular experiments demonstrate that UCNP@PDA@Cy5-pep-cRGD has strong targeted accumulation and enzyme-responsive imaging capability toward tumor cells. In vivo and ex vivo imaging experiments further confirm its ability to visualize MMP-13-responsive activation in microscopic OS lesions and pulmonary metastases. This strategy enables in situ visualization of MMP-13-mediated nanoprobe activation for the identification of microscopic OS lesions and pulmonary metastases.']

title: Exploiting Bridged Conformations for Precise Molecular Recognition in the Design of KRAS-Selective, Orally Available Macrocyclic Peptides.
authors: Mirai Kage; Hatsuo Kawada; Koji Takano; Atsushi Matsuo; Yoshihisa Murata; Satoshi Hashimoto; Minoru Tamiya; Tomoya Kotake; Shino Kuramoto; Takashi Yamano; Machiko Irie; Kazuhiro Ohara; Yuuji Sakurai; Kenichi Nomura; Yuya Morita; Ryuji Hayashi; Yuma Wakamiya; Kana Takei; Hiroshi Tanaka; Yoshikazu Nishimura; Hitoshi Iikura; Takuya Shiraishi; Mikimasa Tanada
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: ['Macrocyclic peptides are attracting attention as a promising therapeutic modality for addressing intracellular targets that are traditionally difficult to address with conventional small molecules or antibodies. In this study, we present the chemical optimization process behind the development of AUBE00 (AP7400, compound 30), a KRAS-selective inhibitor based on a scaffold similar to LUNA18, an orally bioavailable macrocyclic peptide RAS inhibitor. Achieving KRAS isoform selectivity is exceptionally challenging due to the nearly identical backbone structures of KRAS, HRAS, and NRAS (Cα RMSD < 1.1 Å). The success of this study relied on two critical factors: (1) achieving conformational control of the flexible N-alkyl group through a bridging structure linked to the adjacent side chain, which enabled the exploitation of subtle interaction energy differences among the isoforms; and (2) overcoming the trade-off between improved KRAS selectivity and reduced permeability associated with P-glycoprotein (P-gp) substrate liability by employing a modified Caco-2 membrane permeability assay to recover oral bioavailability. Our results demonstrate that a conformational rigidification through a bridged scaffold, implemented while preserving membrane permeability, is a highly effective strategy for achieving isoform selectivity. This study establishes a generalizable design principle for orally bioavailable macrocyclic peptides targeting intracellular proteins that require mutation or isoform selectivity.']
